Exactly the same delay happens with cheques — you record the payment in your cash book the moment you write and send the cheque, but the bank only reduces your account balance once the supplier actually pays it in and it clears. What term describes a cheque that has been written and recorded but not yet cleared through the bank?

examples.correct_understanding: This is an 'unpresented cheque' — recorded immediately in the cash book (reducing its balance) when issued, but not yet deducted from the bank statement balance until the supplier presents it and it clears. This timing difference explains why the cash book balance is temporarily lower than the bank statement balance.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bank charges and standing orders
examples.student_opening: Why does my bank statement show a deduction for 'bank charges' that isn't in my own cash book at all? I never wrote that anywhere.
examples.misconception: Student thinks all transactions must first be recorded by the account holder before appearing in the bank statement, not realising the bank itself can independently apply charges the account holder only learns about upon reconciliation.

turns.text: Why does my bank statement show a deduction for 'bank charges' that isn't in my own cash book at all? I never wrote that anywhere.

Think of a landlord who deducts a small maintenance fee directly from the rent money a caretaker collects on his behalf, without first telling the caretaker in advance. Does the caretaker find out about that deduction only when he checks the final amount handed over, rather than recording it himself beforehand?
Yes, the caretaker would only discover it when he sees the final amount, since he didn't make that deduction himself.

That's exactly how bank charges work — the bank deducts them directly from your account without you initiating or recording the transaction first. Since this only shows up on the bank statement, what should you now do to your OWN cash book to make both records agree?

examples.correct_understanding: Bank charges (and other bank-initiated items like standing orders or direct debits) are deducted by the bank directly, so they appear on the bank statement before the account holder records them. To reconcile, the account holder must UPDATE the cash book by recording the bank charges as a deduction, bringing the cash book balance in line with the adjusted bank statement balance.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, FIFO stock valuation
examples.student_opening: What does it mean when we value closing stock using 'FIFO' — first in, first out? Does it mean the oldest goods are the ones we assume are still sitting unsold in the store?
examples.misconception: Student is uncertain about the direction of the FIFO assumption, unsure whether the oldest or newest goods are considered 'sold first' and which remain as closing stock.

turns.text: What does it mean when we value closing stock using 'FIFO' — first in, first out? Does it mean the oldest goods are the ones we assume are still sitting unsold in the store?

Think of a provisions store owner who always sells from the FRONT of the shelf first — the bags of rice she stocked earliest are placed at the front and sold before the fresher bags stocked later, which sit at the back. Under this habit, which bags of rice would still be left unsold at the end — the ones she stocked EARLIEST, or the ones she stocked MOST RECENTLY?
The most recently stocked bags would be the ones still left, since the earliest ones get sold first.

Exactly — FIFO assumes the OLDEST stock is sold FIRST, so what remains as closing stock are the MOST RECENTLY purchased items. Given that, would closing stock under FIFO be valued using older (often cheaper, in times of rising prices) or newer (often more expensive) purchase prices?

examples.correct_understanding: FIFO (First In, First Out) assumes the earliest (oldest) purchased goods are sold first, so the closing stock consists of the MOST RECENTLY purchased items, valued at their (usually higher, in a period of rising prices) more recent purchase cost.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, lower of cost and net realisable value
examples.student_opening: Some damaged stock cost ₦30,000 to buy but can now only be sold for ₦18,000 after repair costs of ₦2,000. Why can't I just value it in the accounts at what it originally cost, ₦30,000?
examples.misconception: Student assumes stock is always valued at historical cost regardless of current condition, not understanding the prudence concept requires valuing stock at the LOWER of cost and net realisable value.

turns.text: Some damaged stock cost ₦30,000 to buy but can now only be sold for ₦18,000 after repair costs of ₦2,000. Why can't I just value it in the accounts at what it originally cost, ₦30,000?

Think of a trader who bought a bag of tomatoes for ₦5,000 but they've started spoiling, and she can now only sell them quickly for ₦2,000 before they rot completely. If she recorded her stock as still worth ₦5,000 in her account book, would that honestly reflect what she could actually get for them now?
No, that would overstate what the tomatoes are really worth now.

Exactly — accounting follows the prudence concept, which avoids overstating asset values. Given the damaged stock's expected selling price minus any remaining costs (net realisable value) may be LOWER than its original cost, which of the two values — cost, or net realisable value — should be used if it is the smaller one?
The smaller (lower) of the two values should be used.

Right. First calculate the net realisable value: expected selling price minus remaining costs to sell (₦18,000 minus ₦2,000). Then compare that to the original cost of ₦30,000 — which value is lower, and so which should the stock be valued at?

examples.correct_understanding: Net realisable value = Expected selling price - Costs to complete/sell = ₦18,000 - ₦2,000 = ₦16,000. Since ₦16,000 (NRV) is lower than ₦30,000 (cost), the prudence concept requires the stock to be valued at the LOWER figure, ₦16,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, suspense account
examples.student_opening: My trial balance doesn't balance — the debit and credit totals are different. My teacher said to open a 'suspense account'. What is that actually for?
examples.misconception: Student thinks the suspense account 'fixes' or hides the error permanently, not understanding it is a temporary holding account used until the actual error is found and corrected.

turns.text: My trial balance doesn't balance — the debit and credit totals are different. My teacher said to open a 'suspense account'. What is that actually for?

Think of a market association's treasurer counting the day's contributions and finding the total doesn't match what was recorded — instead of pretending it balances or throwing away the discrepancy, he writes down the missing amount separately as 'unexplained difference — to investigate', so the books can still be closed for the day while he looks into it later. Is that difference being ignored, or held aside temporarily?
It's being held aside temporarily, not ignored, until he figures out what caused it.

Exactly what a suspense account does — it temporarily holds the difference so the trial balance totals agree, while you investigate the actual error. Once you find the real cause (say, a transaction posted to the wrong account, or only one side of an entry recorded), what should eventually happen to the suspense account balance?

examples.correct_understanding: A suspense account is a TEMPORARY account used to hold the difference between mismatched trial balance totals, allowing the trial balance to balance while the actual error(s) are investigated. Once the specific error(s) causing the imbalance are found and corrected with proper journal entries, the suspense account balance is cleared to zero.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, errors not revealed by trial balance
examples.student_opening: If my trial balance balances perfectly, does that mean there are definitely no errors in my books?
examples.misconception: Student assumes a balancing trial balance guarantees error-free books, not knowing certain error types (omission, commission, principle, compensating errors) don't affect the trial balance's arithmetic agreement at all.

turns.text: If my trial balance balances perfectly, does that mean there are definitely no errors in my books?

Think of two market women each miscounting their own basket of oranges by 5 — one counts 5 too many, the other counts 5 too few. If you added both their totals together, would the COMBINED total still look correct, even though each individual count was wrong?
The combined total might still look right by coincidence, even though both individual counts were actually wrong.

Exactly — that's a compensating error, where two separate mistakes cancel each other out. Besides that, if a transaction is left out completely from BOTH the debit and credit side (an error of omission), would that also affect whether the trial balance's totals still agree?
No, if it's left out of both sides completely, the totals would still agree even though a transaction is missing.
Right — so given these examples, what would you now say about whether a balancing trial balance guarantees the books are completely free of errors?

examples.correct_understanding: A trial balance balancing does NOT guarantee error-free books. Several error types remain undetected: errors of omission (transaction omitted entirely from both sides), errors of commission (posted to the wrong person's account but correct account type), errors of principle (posted to the wrong class of account), and compensating errors (two errors that cancel each other's effect on the totals).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accrued expenses
examples.student_opening: My shop used electricity in December but the bill only arrived in January, after my financial year ended on 31st December. Do I just ignore it since I haven't paid it yet?
examples.misconception: Student follows a cash-basis mindset, thinking an expense only counts when actually paid, not understanding the accruals concept requires recognising expenses in the period they relate to, whether paid or not.

turns.text: My shop used electricity in December but the bill only arrived in January, after my financial year ended on 31st December. Do I just ignore it since I haven't paid it yet?

Think about a tailor who wears out thread and fabric while sewing dresses in December, even if the fabric supplier doesn't send the invoice until January. Did the tailor actually USE and benefit from that fabric in December, regardless of when the bill arrives?
Yes, she used the fabric in December even though the bill came later.

Exactly — the accruals (matching) concept says an expense belongs to the period in which it was INCURRED (the benefit was used), not necessarily when it's paid. Since the electricity was used in December, should it be included as an expense in December's accounts even though unpaid, and what do we call this kind of unpaid-but-incurred expense?

examples.correct_understanding: Under the accruals concept, expenses are recognised in the period they are incurred, regardless of when payment is made. The December electricity, though unpaid at year-end, must be recorded as an ACCRUED EXPENSE (accrual) — added to December's expenses and shown as a current liability in the balance sheet.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, prepaid expenses
examples.student_opening: I paid ₦120,000 for a full year of shop rent in advance, but only 9 months of my financial year have passed by the time I'm preparing accounts. Should all ₦120,000 appear as this year's rent expense?
examples.misconception: Student thinks a payment made this year should be fully expensed this year, not understanding that the portion relating to a future period must be carried forward as a prepayment (asset), matching expenses to the period they relate to.

turns.text: I paid ₦120,000 for a full year of shop rent in advance, but only 9 months of my financial year have passed by the time I'm preparing accounts. Should all ₦120,000 appear as this year's rent expense?

Think of a farmer who pays a full year's rent on farmland upfront in January, but the farming season he's accounting for only runs through September. Has he actually 'used' the land for the remaining months from October to December yet, even though he already paid for that time?
No, he hasn't used those remaining months yet even though he's already paid for them.

Exactly right — so the portion of the ₦120,000 covering the 3 months NOT yet used (October to December) shouldn't be treated as this year's expense. What should happen to that unused portion in the accounts — should it be expensed anyway, or carried forward as something else?
It should be carried forward as a prepayment, since it relates to the next period.

Correct. Given ₦120,000 covers 12 months (so ₦10,000 per month), how much of that total relates to the 9 months already passed (this year's expense), and how much relates to the remaining 3 months (the prepayment carried forward)?

examples.correct_understanding: Monthly rent = ₦120,000/12 = ₦10,000. This year's expense (9 months) = ₦10,000*9 = ₦90,000. The remaining 3 months (₦10,000*3 = ₦30,000) is a PREPAYMENT, carried forward as a current asset in the balance sheet, not charged as this year's expense.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bad debts and provision for doubtful debts
examples.student_opening: What's the actual difference between 'bad debts written off' and 'provision for doubtful debts'? They both seem to be about customers not paying, just tell me the difference plainly.
examples.misconception: Student treats both terms as identical, not distinguishing between a debt definitely confirmed as unrecoverable (written off completely) versus an estimated, precautionary allowance for debts that MIGHT not be collected.

turns.text: What's the actual difference between 'bad debts written off' and 'provision for doubtful debts'? They both seem to be about customers not paying, just tell me the difference plainly.

Think of a trader who gave goods on credit to two different customers. One customer has since died with no family to pay his debt — that money is definitely gone forever. The other customer has simply been slow to pay and hasn't been seen in the market for a while — he MIGHT still pay eventually, or he might not. Are both situations the same level of certainty?

No, the first one is definitely lost, but the second one is just uncertain, not confirmed as lost. I still don't see how that becomes two different accounting treatments though, please just explain plainly.

Fair, let's narrow it down: because the first debt is DEFINITELY unrecoverable, it is written off completely — removed entirely from debtors and charged as an expense (bad debts). Because the second is only UNCERTAIN (a possibility, not a certainty), the trader can't remove it from debtors yet, since he might still be paid. Instead, what kind of estimated, precautionary amount might the trader set aside for debts that are merely doubtful, without removing them from his debtors list?
Maybe he estimates a percentage that might not be paid and sets it aside separately, but I'm still not fully clear on how it's shown in the accounts.

Let's finish it together: this estimated, precautionary amount is the 'provision for doubtful debts' — it's charged as an expense in the profit and loss account, but on the balance sheet, debtors still appear at their FULL amount, with the provision shown as a DEDUCTION from debtors (not removed from the debtors list like a bad debt is). So bad debts = certain, fully written off; provision for doubtful debts = an estimate, debtors stay listed but shown net of the provision.

examples.correct_understanding: Bad debts written off are debts CONFIRMED as unrecoverable — removed entirely from debtors and charged fully as an expense. Provision for doubtful debts is an ESTIMATED, precautionary allowance for debts that MIGHT become uncollectible — it is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account, but debtors remain shown at their full value in the balance sheet, with the provision deducted from the debtors figure (net presentation), not written off individually.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, gross profit and net profit
examples.student_opening: What's the actual difference between gross profit and net profit? Isn't profit just profit?
examples.misconception: Student treats gross profit and net profit as interchangeable, not distinguishing between profit from trading activity alone versus profit after all other business expenses are deducted.

turns.text: What's the actual difference between gross profit and net profit? Isn't profit just profit?

Think of a trader who buys and resells bags of rice. If she sells a bag for more than she bought it for, that immediate difference is her trading gain from buying and selling alone. But she also has other costs — shop rent, transport, her assistant's wages — that come out of that gain before she knows what she's TRULY left with. Are these two figures (the trading gain alone, versus what's left after all expenses) the same thing?
No, the first is just from buying and selling, but the second is after taking out all her other business costs too.

Exactly that distinction. So which of the two — gross profit or net profit — represents profit purely from trading (sales minus cost of goods sold), and which represents profit AFTER deducting all other operating expenses (rent, wages, etc.)?

examples.correct_understanding: Gross profit = Sales - Cost of goods sold, representing profit purely from trading activity. Net profit = Gross profit - all other operating expenses (rent, wages, utilities, etc.) plus any other income, representing the true overall profit of the business after all costs are accounted for.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, capital and revenue expenditure
examples.student_opening: A shop owner spent ₦500,000 buying a new delivery van and ₦15,000 fuelling it that same month. Why is the ₦500,000 treated completely differently from the ₦15,000 in the accounts?
examples.misconception: Student does not distinguish capital expenditure (creates a long-term asset, benefits multiple years) from revenue expenditure (consumed within the current period), and may want to expense both fully in the same year.

turns.text: A shop owner spent ₦500,000 buying a new delivery van and ₦15,000 fuelling it that same month. Why is the ₦500,000 treated completely differently from the ₦15,000 in the accounts?

Think of a farmer buying a new plough that will last him many farming seasons, versus buying seeds that get used up completely in just ONE season. Should the cost of the plough (useful for years) be treated the same way in his books as the cost of the seeds (used up immediately)?
No, the plough benefits many seasons so it should be treated differently from the seeds which are used up in one season.

Exactly — the van, like the plough, will be used over MANY years, so its ₦500,000 cost is capital expenditure, recorded as a fixed ASSET and spread out (depreciated) over its useful life. The ₦15,000 fuel is used up immediately within the current period. What type of expenditure would you call the fuel cost, and how should it be treated in this year's accounts?

examples.correct_understanding: The ₦500,000 van purchase is CAPITAL EXPENDITURE — it creates a long-term asset that benefits the business over several years, so it's recorded on the balance sheet and depreciated over its useful life, not expensed immediately. The ₦15,000 fuel cost is REVENUE EXPENDITURE — consumed within the current period, charged fully as an expense in this year's profit and loss account.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, classification of assets
examples.student_opening: Why is a delivery van classified as a 'fixed asset' but the stock of goods in the shop classified as a 'current asset'? Aren't both things the business owns and uses? Just tell me the rule.
examples.misconception: Student thinks ownership alone determines asset classification, not understanding the distinction is based on intended use/holding period — long-term use versus short-term conversion to cash.

turns.text: Why is a delivery van classified as a 'fixed asset' but the stock of goods in the shop classified as a 'current asset'? Aren't both things the business owns and uses? Just tell me the rule.

Let's build the rule from something familiar. Think of a trader's own weighing scale that she uses every single day for years to weigh out goods, versus the actual bags of garri sitting on her shelf waiting to be sold and replaced regularly. Is she planning to keep and use the scale for years, the same way she's planning to keep any particular bag of garri for years?
No, she keeps the scale long-term but the garri is sold and replaced quickly. I still don't see the actual accounting rule though, please just state it.

No wahala, let's narrow it down to the rule itself: classification depends on the INTENDED USE and HOLDING PERIOD of the item, not simply what the business owns. If an item is held long-term to help RUN the business (like the scale, or the van), what category does it belong to? And if an item is held short-term, intended to be turned into cash through sale within the normal trading cycle (like the garri, or the stock), what category is that?
I think the scale/van would be fixed assets, and the garri/stock would be current assets, but I want to be sure I've got the full rule right.

You've got it exactly right — let's state the full rule together: FIXED ASSETS are held long-term for use in running the business (not for resale), providing benefit over several years — like the van or the scale. CURRENT ASSETS are intended to be converted into cash within the normal trading cycle (usually within a year) through sale — like stock/garri. The test is always 'how is this item intended to be used and for how long', not simply 'does the business own it'.

examples.correct_understanding: Fixed assets (like the van) are held long-term for use in running the business, not for resale, and provide benefit over several years. Current assets (like stock) are intended to be converted into cash within the normal trading cycle (usually within a year) through sale — the classification depends on intended use/holding period, not merely ownership.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, carriage inwards in trading account
examples.student_opening: Why is 'carriage inwards' of ₦8,000 added to purchases in the trading account, but 'carriage outwards' is treated as a separate expense lower down? I don't get why they're not treated the same, just tell me.
examples.misconception: Student treats carriage inwards and carriage outwards identically, not distinguishing between costs of bringing goods INTO the business (part of cost of purchases) versus costs of delivering goods OUT to customers (a selling/distribution expense).

turns.text: Why is 'carriage inwards' of ₦8,000 added to purchases in the trading account, but 'carriage outwards' is treated as a separate expense lower down? I don't get why they're not treated the same, just tell me.

Think of a trader who pays a transporter to bring bags of rice FROM the wholesaler TO her shop, and later pays a different okada rider to deliver rice FROM her shop TO a customer's house. Is the cost of getting the rice INTO her shop part of what the rice actually cost her to acquire, or is it more like a cost of making a SALE happen?
I think bringing it into the shop is part of getting the rice ready to sell, but I'm still not sure why that changes where it goes in the account, please just tell me directly.

No wahala, let's narrow it down: carriage INWARDS is a cost of acquiring the goods and getting them ready for sale, so it forms part of the cost of purchases in the trading account (added to purchases, before gross profit is calculated). Carriage OUTWARDS happens AFTER the sale, delivering goods to the customer, so it's a selling/distribution expense. Given that difference, where would you expect carriage outwards to appear — in the trading account with purchases, or in the profit and loss section with other expenses?
I think it should be in the profit and loss section since it happens after the sale, but I'm still not 100% sure I'd get this right on my own.

You've got it — let's confirm with the full picture: Trading Account — Purchases ₦? + Carriage Inwards ₦8,000 = Cost of goods available (before deducting closing stock, to get cost of sales, then Sales - Cost of Sales = Gross Profit). Carriage Outwards is NOT part of this; it appears later as a distribution expense in the Profit and Loss Account, deducted from gross profit along with other expenses like rent and wages, to arrive at net profit.

examples.correct_understanding: Carriage inwards is added to purchases in the TRADING ACCOUNT because it is a cost of acquiring/preparing goods for sale (forms part of cost of goods sold). Carriage outwards is a selling and distribution expense incurred AFTER the sale, so it appears in the PROFIT AND LOSS ACCOUNT (deducted from gross profit along with other operating expenses), not added to purchases.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, drawings of goods
examples.student_opening: A shop owner takes goods worth ₦12,000 (at cost) from her own shop for personal home use, without paying for them. How is this recorded, since no cash actually changed hands?
examples.misconception: Student assumes that because no cash was involved, no accounting entry is needed at all, not understanding that drawings of goods must still be recorded to keep the business's records accurate and separate from the owner's personal use.

turns.text: A shop owner takes goods worth ₦12,000 (at cost) from her own shop for personal home use, without paying for them. How is this recorded, since no cash actually changed hands?

Think about the strict separation between a market woman's business basket of goods and her own home kitchen supplies — even though she owns both, mixing them without any record would make it impossible to tell how much stock her BUSINESS actually still has for sale. If she quietly takes some business stock home, has the business's stock level truly stayed the same, cash or no cash?
No, the business's stock has reduced even though no cash was paid, so it needs to be recorded somehow.

Exactly — the business entity concept means the business and owner are treated separately, so this must be recorded. The ₦12,000 worth of goods leaving the business for personal use reduces purchases/stock and represents the owner withdrawing value from the business. What account would you credit to reduce purchases, and which account (representing the owner's withdrawals) would you debit?

examples.correct_understanding: Debit Drawings account ₦12,000 (owner has withdrawn value from the business); Credit Purchases account ₦12,000 (reduces the cost of goods available for sale, since the goods no longer belong to the business's trading stock). This keeps the business's stock/purchases accurate and separate from the owner's personal use.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, contra entries in cash book
examples.student_opening: A trader withdraws ₦25,000 cash from the bank for office use (cash till). Why is this called a 'contra entry' and recorded on BOTH sides of the same cash book?
examples.misconception: Student does not understand that a two-column cash book (cash and bank columns) records both the source and destination of a transfer between cash and bank as separate 'accounts', requiring both a debit and credit within the SAME book.

turns.text: A trader withdraws ₦25,000 cash from the bank for office use (cash till). Why is this called a 'contra entry' and recorded on BOTH sides of the same cash book?

Think of a trader who has money kept in two different safe places — one small box for daily cash sales, and one locked box representing money at the bank. If she physically moves money from the bank box into the cash box, has money left one 'account' (the bank) and arrived in another 'account' (cash), even though both boxes belong to her personally?
Yes, money has moved out of the bank side and into the cash side, even though it's really the same overall money.

Exactly — since a two-column cash book treats 'cash' and 'bank' as two separate accounts within the same book, moving money between them still needs a full double entry: one side increases, the other decreases. Which side of the cash book (cash column or bank column) would be debited to show cash increasing, and which side (bank column) would be credited to show the bank balance decreasing?

examples.correct_understanding: This is a contra entry: Debit Cash column ₦25,000 (cash in hand increases); Credit Bank column ₦25,000 (bank balance decreases), both recorded within the same two-column cash book since cash and bank are treated as separate accounts there, even though the transaction is simply moving the business's own money between its two forms.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, trading and profit and loss account
examples.student_opening: My records show: Sales ₦500,000, Opening Stock ₦40,000, Purchases ₦280,000, Closing Stock ₦60,000, and total expenses ₦90,000. How do I find the net profit?
examples.misconception: Student may jump straight from sales to net profit without first calculating cost of sales and gross profit as separate steps, or may forget to subtract closing stock when finding cost of sales.

turns.text: My records show: Sales ₦500,000, Opening Stock ₦40,000, Purchases ₦280,000, Closing Stock ₦60,000, and total expenses ₦90,000. How do I find the net profit?

Recall the firewood seller idea: to know the cost of what was actually SOLD (not just bought), you take opening stock plus purchases, then subtract what's left unsold (closing stock). What is the cost of sales using your opening stock, purchases, and closing stock figures?
Correct. Now find gross profit (Sales - Cost of sales), and then subtract the total expenses from gross profit to find net profit — what are your two final figures?

examples.correct_understanding: Cost of sales = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock = ₦40,000 + ₦280,000 - ₦60,000 = ₦260,000. Gross profit = Sales - Cost of sales = ₦500,000 - ₦260,000 = ₦240,000. Net profit = Gross profit - Expenses = ₦240,000 - ₦90,000 = ₦150,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, goodwill on admission of a partner
examples.student_opening: Goodwill of ₦90,000 was raised and credited to old partners Bello and Chika (who shared profits equally) when Dayo was admitted. Why is this goodwill often then written OFF again, shared among ALL THREE partners in the NEW ratio?
examples.misconception: Student does not understand that raising goodwill and then writing it off in the new ratio is a common method to avoid keeping an intangible goodwill account permanently on the books, while still fairly compensating the old partners first.

turns.text: Goodwill of ₦90,000 was raised and credited to old partners Bello and Chika (who shared profits equally) when Dayo was admitted. Why is this goodwill often then written OFF again, shared among ALL THREE partners in the NEW ratio?

Think of it as two separate steps in fairness. First, before Dayo joins, Bello and Chika are compensated for the reputation and value they built — that's step one, sharing goodwill in the OLD ratio between just the two of them. But many partnerships don't want an intangible 'goodwill' figure sitting permanently in the books. What would writing that goodwill amount back OFF, shared among all three partners in the NEW ratio, actually achieve?
It removes the goodwill figure from the books afterward, but now all three partners including Dayo share in writing it off?

Exactly — crediting goodwill to the old partners (old ratio) first, then debiting (writing off) that same goodwill among ALL partners (new ratio) has a net effect: it transfers value from the new partner to the old partners without keeping a permanent goodwill account. Why does this two-step approach ensure Dayo effectively pays his share of goodwill to Bello and Chika, even though no goodwill account remains?

examples.correct_understanding: Step 1: Goodwill ₦90,000 is credited to Bello and Chika equally (old ratio) = ₦45,000 each, compensating them for value built before Dayo's admission. Step 2: The same ₦90,000 goodwill is then written off (debited) to ALL THREE partners in the NEW profit-sharing ratio. The net effect is that Dayo's capital account is reduced by his share of goodwill (effectively paying for it), while Bello and Chika retain a net benefit — all without a goodwill account remaining permanently on the balance sheet.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, straight line depreciation
examples.student_opening: A delivery van costs ₦600,000, has an estimated scrap value of ₦50,000, and is expected to last 5 years. How do I find the annual depreciation using the straight line method?
examples.misconception: Student may forget to subtract the scrap (residual) value before dividing by useful life, treating the full cost as the amount to be depreciated.

turns.text: A delivery van costs ₦600,000, has an estimated scrap value of ₦50,000, and is expected to last 5 years. How do I find the annual depreciation using the straight line method?

Think of a water pot that a family expects to still be able to sell for scrap clay value even after years of use — they wouldn't expect to lose the ENTIRE original price over its life, only the difference between what they paid and what it's worth as scrap at the end. What amount actually represents the TOTAL value the van will lose over its life, given it won't be worthless at the end?
The difference between the cost and the scrap value, so ₦600,000 minus ₦50,000.
Correct — that's the depreciable amount. Now divide that depreciable amount by the number of years of useful life to spread it evenly — what is the annual depreciation?

examples.correct_understanding: Depreciable amount = Cost - Scrap value = ₦600,000 - ₦50,000 = ₦550,000. Annual depreciation (straight line) = ₦550,000/5 = ₦110,000 per year.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, disposal of fixed assets
examples.student_opening: An old machine with a book value (net of accumulated depreciation) of ₦45,000 is sold for ₦60,000. Is the extra ₦15,000 treated as sales revenue, since we received more cash than the asset's value?
examples.misconception: Student confuses the proceeds from selling a fixed asset with ordinary trading revenue (sales), not understanding it should instead be recognised as a profit on disposal, separate from trading income.

turns.text: An old machine with a book value (net of accumulated depreciation) of ₦45,000 is sold for ₦60,000. Is the extra ₦15,000 treated as sales revenue, since we received more cash than the asset's value?

Think about a farmer selling his old plough after years of use, for more than its estimated remaining worth. Is he running a 'plough-selling business' the way he runs his farming-produce-selling business, or is this a one-off event involving equipment he no longer needs?
It's a one-off event with his equipment, not part of his normal produce-selling business.

Exactly — selling a fixed asset is not part of normal trading activity, so the ₦15,000 shouldn't be treated as sales revenue. Since the machine was sold for MORE than its book value, what would you call that ₦15,000 difference in the accounts?

examples.correct_understanding: The ₦15,000 excess of sale proceeds (₦60,000) over the asset's net book value (₦45,000) is recognised as a PROFIT ON DISPOSAL of fixed asset, shown in the profit and loss account as other income — separate from ordinary trading sales revenue, since selling a fixed asset is not part of the business's normal trading activity.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, choice of depreciation method
examples.student_opening: Why would a business choose reducing balance depreciation instead of straight line for a delivery vehicle? I don't see why the method should even matter, just tell me which one is 'correct'.
examples.misconception: Student thinks there is one universally 'correct' depreciation method, not understanding the choice should reflect the pattern of how an asset actually loses value/usefulness over time.

turns.text: Why would a business choose reducing balance depreciation instead of straight line for a delivery vehicle? I don't see why the method should even matter, just tell me which one is 'correct'.

Think about a new okada motorcycle — does it typically lose a bigger chunk of its value in the very first year or two of heavy use, or does it lose value at a perfectly steady, equal amount every single year of its life?
I think it probably loses more value early on when it's newest, but I still don't see why that means one method is better, please just tell me which is correct.

No wahala, let's narrow it down: there isn't one universally 'correct' method — the goal is to match the depreciation CHARGE to the actual PATTERN of how the asset loses usefulness. If a vehicle genuinely loses more value in early years (heavy early wear, faster obsolescence) and less in later years, which method — straight line (equal charge every year) or reducing balance (bigger charge early, smaller later) — better reflects that real pattern?
Reducing balance seems to match that pattern better, but I'm still not fully confident explaining why in my own words.

You've reasoned it correctly — let's confirm it fully: reducing balance depreciation charges a larger amount in the earlier years (applied to a bigger remaining book value) and progressively smaller amounts later, which suits assets like vehicles that lose value fastest when new. Straight line depreciation is better suited to assets that lose value fairly evenly over time (like a building with a steady, predictable pattern of wear). The 'right' method depends on which pattern most realistically reflects how the specific asset is used up.

examples.correct_understanding: There is no single universally correct depreciation method — the choice should reflect the asset's actual pattern of value loss. Reducing balance suits assets that lose more value earlier (like vehicles, due to heavy early wear/faster obsolescence), while straight line suits assets that lose value steadily and evenly over their useful life (like buildings).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bank reconciliation statement
examples.student_opening: My cash book balance is ₦85,000 but my bank statement shows ₦102,000. There's an unpresented cheque of ₦30,000 and a bank lodgement of ₦13,000 not yet credited by the bank. How do I reconcile the two accounts?
examples.misconception: Student is unsure whether to add or subtract the unpresented cheque and uncredited lodgement when starting from the bank statement balance versus the cash book balance, often applying both adjustments the wrong way round.

turns.text: My cash book balance is ₦85,000 but my bank statement shows ₦102,000. There's an unpresented cheque of ₦30,000 and a bank lodgement of ₦13,000 not yet credited by the bank. How do I reconcile the two accounts?

Let's reason from the bank statement's point of view. The unpresented cheque has already been deducted in YOUR cash book, but the bank hasn't deducted it yet since the supplier hasn't cashed it. So starting from the bank statement balance, should you add or subtract the unpresented cheque to reflect what the balance WILL become once the bank catches up?
I should subtract it from the bank statement balance, since the bank hasn't deducted it yet but eventually will.

Correct. Now for the ₦13,000 lodgement already recorded as received in YOUR cash book, but not yet appearing on the bank statement — should you add or subtract that from the bank statement balance to get it in line with your cash book?
Add it, since the bank hasn't recorded it yet but it will show up eventually.

Exactly right. Starting from the bank statement balance of ₦102,000, subtract the unpresented cheque and add the uncredited lodgement — what final adjusted balance do you get, and does it match the cash book balance of ₦85,000?

examples.correct_understanding: Adjusted bank balance = ₦102,000 - ₦30,000 (unpresented cheque) + ₦13,000 (uncredited lodgement) = ₦85,000, which matches the cash book balance of ₦85,000, confirming the reconciliation.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, dishonoured cheques
examples.student_opening: A customer's cheque for ₦18,000 which I already recorded as received and banked has now 'bounced' (dishonoured) due to insufficient funds. What do I need to do to my cash book now?
examples.misconception: Student thinks once a cheque is recorded as received, the entry stands permanently regardless of what happens afterward, not realising a dishonoured cheque must be reversed since the money was never actually received.

turns.text: A customer's cheque for ₦18,000 which I already recorded as received and banked has now 'bounced' (dishonoured) due to insufficient funds. What do I need to do to my cash book now?

Think of a trader who happily recorded a customer's payment as received, only to later find out the customer's promise to pay was actually empty — the money never truly arrived in her purse. If she already recorded the money as received, but it turns out that never really happened, should her record stay as is, or does it need correcting?
It needs correcting since the money never actually came in, even though she first recorded it as received.

Exactly right. Since the ₦18,000 was originally debited into the cash book (bank column) when the cheque was first received, and it turns out that money isn't really there, what entry would you now need to make to reverse that, and what happens to the customer's debtor balance as a result?

examples.correct_understanding: The dishonoured cheque must be reversed: Credit Bank column ₦18,000 (reducing the bank balance back down, since the money was never really received), and Debit the customer's account ₦18,000 (reinstating them as a debtor, since they still owe the business the money).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, weighted average cost method
examples.student_opening: How is the 'weighted average cost' method of stock valuation different from FIFO, if both are just ways of pricing closing stock?
examples.misconception: Student thinks weighted average simply means taking a straightforward average of purchase prices without considering the different quantities bought at each price.

turns.text: How is the 'weighted average cost' method of stock valuation different from FIFO, if both are just ways of pricing closing stock?

Think of a garri seller who buys 8 bags at ₦4,000 each and later buys only 2 more bags at ₦5,000 each, then mixes them all together in one big storage bin so you can no longer tell which bag came from which purchase. If you wanted one single fair price per bag from that mixed bin, would you just average ₦4,000 and ₦5,000 equally (giving ₦4,500), or would you need to account for the fact that far MORE bags were bought at ₦4,000 than at ₦5,000?
You'd need to account for how many bags were bought at each price, not just average the two prices equally.

Exactly — that's why it's called WEIGHTED average, weighting each price by the quantity bought at it, unlike FIFO which assumes specific batches are sold in a specific order. Given the garri seller's mixed bin, would the weighted average price per bag be closer to {N}4,000 or exactly halfway between {N}4,000 and {N}5,000, given most bags cost {N}4,000?

examples.correct_understanding: Weighted average cost values stock by dividing the TOTAL cost of all units available by the TOTAL number of units, weighting each purchase price by its quantity — unlike FIFO, which assumes goods are sold/used in the order purchased and tracks specific cost layers. Since most units in this example were bought at the lower price, the weighted average would be closer to that lower price, not a simple midpoint average of the two prices.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, preparing a trial balance
examples.student_opening: When preparing a trial balance, how do I know whether an account balance (like rent expense, or capital) should be listed in the debit column or the credit column?
examples.misconception: Student tries to memorise a fixed list of account names for each column rather than understanding the underlying rule based on the account's normal balance (asset/expense = debit; liability/capital/income = credit).

turns.text: When preparing a trial balance, how do I know whether an account balance (like rent expense, or capital) should be listed in the debit column or the credit column?

Think of a market woman's simple mental rule: things she OWNS or SPENDS on sit on one side of her thinking, and things she OWES or has been GIVEN by others sit on the other side. If capital represents what the OWNER has invested into the business (money the business effectively 'owes back' to the owner), would you expect it to behave more like something owned, or something owed?
More like something owed, since the business owes that value back to the owner.
Good reasoning — capital, like liabilities, normally carries a CREDIT balance. Now think about rent expense — is that something the business owns/uses up, or something it owes to someone else?
Something it uses up, an expense, so maybe that's a debit balance instead.

Exactly right. Based on that reasoning — assets and expenses normally have one type of balance, while liabilities, capital, and income normally have the other — which column (debit or credit) would each of those two categories appear in on the trial balance?

examples.correct_understanding: Assets and expenses normally carry DEBIT balances (they represent what the business owns or has consumed). Liabilities, capital, and income normally carry CREDIT balances (they represent what the business owes to others, including its owner). Understanding this underlying rule, rather than memorising each account by name, correctly places any account in the trial balance.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, correction of errors via journal entries
examples.student_opening: A ₦7,000 payment for office stationery was wrongly debited to the Office Equipment account instead of the Stationery (expense) account. How do I correct this with a journal entry? I don't know how to reverse a wrong entry, just show me what to write.
examples.misconception: Student does not understand that correcting an error posted to the wrong account requires a journal entry that removes it from the wrong account (credit) and places it in the correct account (debit), not simply deleting the original entry.

turns.text: A ₦7,000 payment for office stationery was wrongly debited to the Office Equipment account instead of the Stationery (expense) account. How do I correct this with a journal entry? I don't know how to reverse a wrong entry, just show me what to write.

Think of a market trader who mistakenly wrote a debt of ₦7,000 in her NEIGHBOUR's account book instead of her OWN. To fix it, would she just scribble it out silently, or would she need to clearly record taking it OUT of the wrong book and putting it INTO the correct one?

She'd need to clearly record removing it from the wrong place and adding it to the right place, but I still don't know which side (debit or credit) does which in this accounting case, please just show me.

No wahala, let's narrow it down: since the ₦7,000 was WRONGLY debited to Office Equipment, to remove it from there you must do the OPPOSITE — credit Office Equipment ₦7,000. Then, since it belongs in Stationery expense, you debit Stationery ₦7,000 to place it correctly. Can you see why crediting the wrong account 'cancels' the original wrong debit?
I think crediting it cancels out the wrong debit since they're opposite, but I'm still not fully confident writing the full journal entry myself.

Let's write it out together: Journal entry — Debit Stationery Account ₦7,000; Credit Office Equipment Account ₦7,000; narration: 'Correction of stationery expense wrongly debited to Office Equipment.' This removes the ₦7,000 from the asset account (where it doesn't belong) and correctly records it as an expense.

examples.correct_understanding: Journal entry to correct the error: Debit Stationery (expense) account ₦7,000; Credit Office Equipment account ₦7,000, with a narration explaining the correction. This removes the amount from the incorrect asset account and correctly records it as an expense.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, returns inwards and returns outwards
examples.student_opening: What's the difference between 'returns inwards' and 'returns outwards', and why do they get deducted from sales and purchases respectively instead of just being ignored? Just tell me plainly, I keep mixing them up.
examples.misconception: Student is unsure which direction of goods movement each term refers to, and does not understand why returns must reduce the original sales/purchases figures rather than being left out of the accounts.

turns.text: What's the difference between 'returns inwards' and 'returns outwards', and why do they get deducted from sales and purchases respectively instead of just being ignored? Just tell me plainly, I keep mixing them up.

Let's ground it in something concrete. Think of a tailor who sold a dress to a customer, but the customer brings it back because of a bad stitch — that dress is coming BACK INTO the tailor's shop. Separately, the tailor herself once returned some bad fabric back OUT to her cloth supplier. In which direction is each of these movements — into the business, or out of the business?
I think the dress comes in and the fabric goes out, but I still keep forgetting which one is called 'inwards' and which is 'outwards' in the accounts, please just tell me directly.

No wahala, let's fix the naming directly: 'returns INWARDS' are goods coming back INTO the business FROM customers (like the dress) — these reduce SALES. 'Returns OUTWARDS' are goods the business sends back OUT to its suppliers (like the fabric) — these reduce PURCHASES. Now, since the dress was originally counted as a completed sale, but the customer no longer has it, should it still count as a full sale in the accounts?
No, it shouldn't still count as a full sale since it didn't really go through in the end, but I want to make sure I've got the full picture right now.

You've got it — let's confirm the complete picture: Returns inwards are deducted from gross sales to get NET SALES (since those goods came back and the sale didn't stick). Returns outwards are deducted from gross purchases to get NET PURCHASES (since those goods were sent back and never became part of what the business actually kept). Both adjustments keep the trading account showing only the goods genuinely sold or genuinely bought and retained.

examples.correct_understanding: Returns inwards (sales returns) are goods returned BY customers, deducted from gross sales to find net sales, since the sale did not ultimately go through. Returns outwards (purchases returns) are goods the business sends BACK to its suppliers, deducted from gross purchases to find net purchases, since those goods are no longer part of what the business actually kept and paid for.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, total cost of production worked example
examples.student_opening: A factory recorded: Direct materials ₦120,000, Direct labour ₦70,000, Direct expenses ₦10,000, Factory rent ₦25,000, Factory power ₦15,000. How do I organise these into prime cost and total production cost?
examples.misconception: Student may lump all costs together into one total without separating direct costs (which form prime cost) from indirect factory overheads (added after prime cost), losing the layered structure required in a manufacturing account.

turns.text: A factory recorded: Direct materials ₦120,000, Direct labour ₦70,000, Direct expenses ₦10,000, Factory rent ₦25,000, Factory power ₦15,000. How do I organise these into prime cost and total production cost?

Recall the tailor and adire gown idea — the cloth, her direct sewing hours, and any cost paid specifically FOR that one gown (like a special dye) are all DIRECT costs. Workshop rent and electricity benefit ALL her work generally, so they're INDIRECT. Looking at the five items given, which three would you group together as DIRECT costs forming prime cost?
Direct materials, direct labour, and direct expenses — those three should form prime cost.

Correct. Add those three together first to get prime cost, then add the remaining two (factory rent and factory power, which are indirect factory overheads) to prime cost — what is your prime cost, and what is your total production cost?

examples.correct_understanding: Prime cost = Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses = ₦120,000 + ₦70,000 + ₦10,000 = ₦200,000. Total production cost = Prime cost + Factory overheads (rent + power) = ₦200,000 + ₦25,000 + ₦15,000 = ₦240,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, going concern concept
examples.student_opening: Why do we value a shop's fixed assets at their cost less depreciation in the accounts, instead of what they'd sell for if the shop closed down today?
examples.misconception: Student assumes assets should always be valued at their immediate resale/liquidation value, not understanding the going concern concept assumes the business will continue operating, so assets are valued for continued use, not forced sale.

turns.text: Why do we value a shop's fixed assets at their cost less depreciation in the accounts, instead of what they'd sell for if the shop closed down today?

Think of a family's cooking pots and grinding stones — if you valued them by what a scrap dealer would pay for them TODAY, would that reflect their true worth to the family who plans to keep cooking with them for many more years?
No, that scrap value would be much lower than what they're actually worth to the family who keeps using them.

Exactly — accounting assumes a business will CONTINUE operating into the foreseeable future (the going concern concept), so assets are valued based on their usefulness for continued operation (cost less depreciation), not forced/liquidation sale value. Under what different circumstance might it actually become appropriate to switch to valuing assets at their break-up/liquidation value instead?

examples.correct_understanding: The going concern concept assumes a business will continue operating for the foreseeable future, so assets are valued at cost less accumulated depreciation (reflecting ongoing use), not at forced-sale/liquidation value. Liquidation value would only become appropriate if there were genuine doubt about the business continuing (e.g. impending closure or insolvency).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, partners' capital and current accounts
examples.student_opening: Why do partnerships often keep two separate accounts for each partner — a 'capital account' and a 'current account' — instead of just one combined account?
examples.misconception: Student sees the split as unnecessary duplication, not understanding that capital accounts record the fixed, long-term investment while current accounts record the frequently changing items (salary, interest, drawings, profit share) each year.

turns.text: Why do partnerships often keep two separate accounts for each partner — a 'capital account' and a 'current account' — instead of just one combined account?

Think of a family compound where the LAND itself (the fixed, foundational asset the family owns) is recorded separately from the day-to-day list of who contributed what to this month's feast, who took food out, and who's owed what from this month's contributions. Would it be confusing to lump the permanent land ownership record together with the constantly changing monthly feast contributions?
Yes, it would be confusing to mix something permanent with something that changes every month.

Exactly the reason for the split. The capital account holds each partner's original, fairly FIXED long-term investment (rarely changing), while items like salary, interest on capital, interest on drawings, share of profit, and actual drawings change every year. Which of the two accounts — capital or current — would you expect to record these frequently changing yearly items?

examples.correct_understanding: The capital account records each partner's fixed, long-term capital investment in the business, which rarely changes. The current account records the frequently changing yearly items — salary, interest on capital, interest on drawings, share of profit/loss, and drawings — keeping the permanent capital stake clearly separate from the fluctuating annual entitlements and withdrawals.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, partner's current account
examples.student_opening: Partner Ibrahim's current account starts the year with a credit balance of ₦15,000. During the year he is credited with salary ₦30,000, interest on capital ₦8,000, and profit share ₦42,000, but he made drawings of ₦50,000 (debited). What is his current account balance at the end of the year? I keep mixing up which entries are debits and which are credits, just tell me the final figure.
examples.misconception: Student is unsure whether salary, interest on capital, and profit share increase or decrease the current account balance relative to drawings, and may add everything together without distinguishing credits from debits.

turns.text: Partner Ibrahim's current account starts the year with a credit balance of ₦15,000. During the year he is credited with salary ₦30,000, interest on capital ₦8,000, and profit share ₦42,000, but he made drawings of ₦50,000 (debited). What is his current account balance at the end of the year? I keep mixing up which entries are debits and which are credits, just tell me the final figure.

Let's separate what INCREASES Ibrahim's entitlement from what DECREASES it. Salary, interest on capital, and profit share are all amounts the business owes TO him for his contribution and work — would you expect these to be credited (increasing what's owed to him) or debited?
Credited, since they increase what the business owes him. But drawings confuse me, please just give me the final number.

No wahala, let's narrow it down: drawings are money he has already TAKEN OUT of the business for himself, so they reduce what the business still owes him — drawings are DEBITED to his current account. So you need to ADD all the credit items (opening balance, salary, interest, profit share) and then SUBTRACT the debit item (drawings). What is the total of the credit items first?
₦15,000 + ₦30,000 + ₦8,000 + ₦42,000... let me try... that's ₦95,000, but I'm still not confident about the final subtraction step.

Your addition is correct — let's finish it together: total credits = ₦95,000. Subtract the drawings (debit) of ₦50,000: ₦95,000 - ₦50,000 = ₦45,000. So Ibrahim's current account ends the year with a CREDIT balance of ₦45,000, meaning the business still owes him that amount, which would typically be carried forward or paid out.

examples.correct_understanding: Total credits to Ibrahim's current account = Opening balance ₦15,000 + Salary ₦30,000 + Interest on capital ₦8,000 + Profit share ₦42,000 = ₦95,000. Less drawings (debit) ₦50,000 = closing balance of ₦45,000 (credit), representing the amount still owed to Ibrahim by the business at year end.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, receipts and payments account vs income and expenditure account
examples.student_opening: Our teacher said clubs prepare a receipts and payments account AND an income and expenditure account. Abi it's the same thing? Both are just money in and money out.
examples.misconception: Student thinks the receipts and payments account and the income and expenditure account are the same statement with different names.

turns.text: Our teacher said clubs prepare a receipts and payments account AND an income and expenditure account. Abi it's the same thing? Both are just money in and money out.

Picture the harvest committee in your church. The treasurer has a notebook where she writes every naira that physically entered or left the church purse this year — including the ₦50,000 paid for a new keyboard that will be used for many years. Now if the parish priest asks 'did this year's activities actually cover this year's costs?', would that notebook alone answer him fairly?
Hmm, not really. The keyboard will serve for years, so putting all of it in this year makes this year look bad.

Good thinking. So one statement is simply a summary of cash movements, whatever year or purpose they relate to. The other tries to match only THIS year's income against THIS year's expenses. Which of the two names do you think describes the cash notebook, and which describes the 'did we cover our costs' statement?
The receipts and payments account is the cash notebook, and the income and expenditure account is the one that matches this year's income and expenses.

That's the distinction. Now push it one step: since the income and expenditure account follows the accruals concept, what would you expect it to do with the keyboard instead of charging the full ₦50,000 this year?

examples.correct_understanding: The receipts and payments account is a summary of the cash book (all cash received and paid, capital or revenue, any period), starting with the opening cash/bank balance and ending with the closing balance. The income and expenditure account is prepared on an accruals basis like a profit and loss account, including only revenue income and expenditure of the period (e.g. depreciation on the keyboard rather than its full cost), and shows a surplus or deficit.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, receipts and payments account
examples.student_opening: Town union account: cash at start of year ₦45,000. Received: levies ₦120,000, donations ₦30,000, bazaar ₦55,000. Paid: hall rent ₦60,000, refreshments ₦25,000, plastic chairs ₦80,000. What is the closing cash balance? I got ₦40,000.
examples.misconception: Student subtracts payments from receipts but forgets to start from the opening cash balance.

turns.text: Town union account: cash at start of year ₦45,000. Received: levies ₦120,000, donations ₦30,000, bazaar ₦55,000. Paid: hall rent ₦60,000, refreshments ₦25,000, plastic chairs ₦80,000. What is the closing cash balance? I got ₦40,000.

Think of the town union treasurer's cash box. On the first day of the year she opened it and there was already ₦45,000 inside, left over from last year. Then money came in and money went out. If you only compare what came in with what went out this year, have you accounted for everything that is in the box?
I don't get it. Receipts minus payments is what I did. Just tell me what I'm missing, abeg.

No wahala, let me narrow it. Your ₦40,000 is correct as the EXCESS of receipts over payments for the year. But the box didn't start empty. The receipts and payments account always opens with the balance b/d. So the closing figure = balance at start + total receipts − total payments. What is ₦45,000 + ₦205,000 − ₦165,000?
Wait, so ₦205,000 is the total receipts... I'm still confused about where the ₦45,000 enters.

Let's lay it out together. Balance b/d ₦45,000. Add receipts: ₦120,000 + ₦30,000 + ₦55,000 = ₦205,000, so cash available = ₦250,000. Less payments: ₦60,000 + ₦25,000 + ₦80,000 = ₦165,000. Closing cash balance c/d = ₦250,000 − ₦165,000 = ₦85,000. Your ₦40,000 was the year's net inflow; adding the ₦45,000 the treasurer started with gives the ₦85,000 she should find in the box.

examples.correct_understanding: Closing cash = opening balance ₦45,000 + receipts ₦205,000 − payments ₦165,000 = ₦85,000. The receipts and payments account starts with the opening cash balance; the ₦40,000 excess of receipts over payments is only the year's net movement.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accumulated fund
examples.student_opening: Old students' association at 1 January: equipment ₦150,000, cash ₦20,000, subscriptions in arrears ₦6,000, subscriptions in advance ₦4,000, rent accrued ₦10,000. I added everything to get the accumulated fund — ₦190,000. Is that right?
examples.misconception: Student treats subscriptions in advance as an asset and adds it to the accumulated fund instead of deducting it as a liability.

turns.text: Old students' association at 1 January: equipment ₦150,000, cash ₦20,000, subscriptions in arrears ₦6,000, subscriptions in advance ₦4,000, rent accrued ₦10,000. I added everything to get the accumulated fund — ₦190,000. Is that right?

Imagine you are the association's financial secretary. Some old boys owe dues for last year — they will pay you later. Other old boys paid NEXT year's dues early — you are holding their money but you still owe them a year of membership. Of those two groups, which one is the association owed by, and which one is the association owing to?
The ones in arrears owe us. The ones who paid in advance... we owe them the membership, so it's like we're holding their money.

Exactly. So subscriptions in advance behave like a liability, the same as the rent the association hasn't paid yet. The accumulated fund is the club's version of capital: what it owns minus what it owes. Can you split your list into assets and liabilities and redo the sum?

That's it. Notice your first answer of ₦190,000 was wrong by exactly twice the liabilities — once for adding them instead of subtracting. Why do you think examiners like to ask for the opening accumulated fund before anything else in a club question?

examples.correct_understanding: Accumulated fund = assets − liabilities = (₦150,000 + ₦20,000 + ₦6,000) − (₦4,000 + ₦10,000) = ₦162,000. Subscriptions in advance and accrued rent are liabilities; subscriptions in arrears is an asset.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, subscriptions in arrears and in advance
examples.student_opening: Our old students' association received ₦80,000 dues in 2024. Out of it, ₦5,000 was for 2023 and ₦3,000 was for 2025. Members still owe ₦7,000 for 2024. My answer for subscription income in the income and expenditure account is ₦80,000.
examples.misconception: Student uses the full cash received as subscription income without removing last year's arrears and next year's advance, or adding this year's unpaid dues.

turns.text: Our old students' association received ₦80,000 dues in 2024. Out of it, ₦5,000 was for 2023 and ₦3,000 was for 2025. Members still owe ₦7,000 for 2024. My answer for subscription income in the income and expenditure account is ₦80,000.

Think of an Aso-ebi coordinator for a 2024 wedding. Some people paid in 2024 for LAST year's wedding they owed, some paid in 2024 for next year's wedding, and some who wore this year's fabric haven't paid yet. If you want to know how much was really earned from THIS year's wedding, which of those three groups would you remove, and which would you add back?
Remove the payment for last year's wedding and the one for next year. Add the people who haven't paid for this year yet.
Now translate that directly to the association's dues. Start from ₦80,000 and apply those three adjustments. What figure do you get?

Correct. Here is how the subscriptions account proves your ₦79,000; the income figure is the balancing item:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (arrears) | 5,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 80,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 79,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in advance) | 3,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in arrears) |  | 7,000 |
|  | Total | 87,000 | 87,000 |
Which of the two closing balances would you show as a current asset in the balance sheet, and which as a current liability?

examples.correct_understanding: Subscription income = cash received ₦80,000 − arrears for 2023 ₦5,000 − advance for 2025 ₦3,000 + arrears for 2024 ₦7,000 = ₦79,000. The ₦7,000 arrears is a current asset and the ₦3,000 in advance is a current liability.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, subscriptions in advance
examples.student_opening: If members pay next year's dues this year, the money is already in our bank. So why won't we count it as this year's income?
examples.misconception: Student thinks subscriptions received in advance are income of the current year because the cash has already been received.

turns.text: If members pay next year's dues this year, the money is already in our bank. So why won't we count it as this year's income?
Suppose you pay your PTA levy for next term today, and the school collapses before next term starts. Would you say the school had already 'earned' your money, or would you expect a refund?
I would want my money back. They haven't done anything for it yet.

Exactly — the school owes you a service it hasn't delivered. So for the club, money received for next year's membership is something the club still OWES its members. In the balance sheet, where would you put something the club owes?
Under liabilities. So subscriptions in advance are a current liability, not income for this year.
Good. Now, which accounting concept is at work here — the one that says income should be recognised in the period it is earned, not when the cash is received?

examples.correct_understanding: Subscriptions received in advance are not income of the current year; under the accruals (matching) concept they belong to next year and are shown as a current liability in the balance sheet (statement of financial position) of the club.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, subscriptions account
examples.student_opening: Social club: subscriptions in arrears at 1 Jan ₦4,000, in advance at 1 Jan ₦2,500. Cash received during the year ₦96,000. At 31 Dec, arrears ₦6,000, in advance ₦3,500. Find subscriptions for the income and expenditure account. This one has four adjustments and I'm lost.
examples.misconception: Student cannot decide on which side of the subscriptions account opening arrears and opening advance go, and so cannot find the income figure.

turns.text: Social club: subscriptions in arrears at 1 Jan ₦4,000, in advance at 1 Jan ₦2,500. Cash received during the year ₦96,000. At 31 Dec, arrears ₦6,000, in advance ₦3,500. Find subscriptions for the income and expenditure account. This one has four adjustments and I'm lost.

Think of the social club like a gym at the end of the street. At the start of the year, some members owed old fees (the gym is owed), and some had prepaid (the gym owes them this year's service, which it will now deliver). Which of those two opening groups gives the gym MORE income to recognise this year without new cash coming in?
I don't know, honestly. All these arrears and advance are scattering my head. Please just tell me the answer.

I hear you, it's a lot at once. One step: the ₦2,500 paid in advance LAST year is membership being enjoyed THIS year, so it is added to this year's income. The ₦4,000 opening arrears was last year's income being collected now, so it is taken OUT of this year's cash. Try: ₦96,000 − ₦4,000 + ₦2,500, then handle the two closing figures the opposite way. What do you get?
₦96,000 − ₦4,000 + ₦2,500 = ₦94,500. But for the closing ones I don't know which to add.

Let's finish it with the account itself:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (arrears) | 4,000 |  |
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (in advance) |  | 2,500 |
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 96,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 97,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in advance) | 3,500 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in arrears) |  | 6,000 |
|  | Total | 104,500 | 104,500 |
Reading it: closing arrears (₦6,000) is this year's income not yet received, so it is added; closing advance (₦3,500) is cash for next year, so it is removed. ₦94,500 + ₦6,000 − ₦3,500 = ₦97,000, the balancing figure transferred to the income and expenditure account.

examples.correct_understanding: Subscription income = ₦96,000 − opening arrears ₦4,000 + opening advance ₦2,500 + closing arrears ₦6,000 − closing advance ₦3,500 = ₦97,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, surplus and deficit
examples.student_opening: In my answer for the Social Club I wrote 'Net profit ₦24,000 added to capital'. My teacher crossed it. Why? The figure was correct.
examples.misconception: Student uses 'net profit' and 'capital' for a non-profit organisation instead of 'surplus/deficit' and 'accumulated fund'.

turns.text: In my answer for the Social Club I wrote 'Net profit ₦24,000 added to capital'. My teacher crossed it. Why? The figure was correct.

When your town union holds its end-of-year meeting, does anyone stand up to share the 'profit' among the members like shareholders sharing dividends, or is the extra money simply kept in the union's purse for future projects?
They keep it for the next project, like the village borehole. Nobody shares it.

Right — the union doesn't exist to make profit for owners. So accountants use different words for a club. What do you think they call the excess of income over expenditure, and what do they call the club's 'capital'?
The excess is a surplus, and if expenses are more it's a deficit. The capital is... the accumulated fund?
Exactly. So how would you now rewrite your line so the examiner gives you the mark?

examples.correct_understanding: In non-profit organisations, excess of income over expenditure is called a surplus (the opposite is a deficit), and the capital is called the accumulated fund. The correct phrasing is 'Surplus ₦24,000 added to accumulated fund'.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bar trading account
examples.student_opening: The club's bar: sales ₦180,000, opening bar stock ₦15,000, bar purchases ₦110,000, closing bar stock ₦20,000, bar steward's wages ₦12,000. I said profit is ₦180,000 − ₦110,000 − ₦12,000 = ₦58,000.
examples.misconception: Student forgets to compute cost of bar sales using opening and closing bar stock and deducts only bar purchases.

turns.text: The club's bar: sales ₦180,000, opening bar stock ₦15,000, bar purchases ₦110,000, closing bar stock ₦20,000, bar steward's wages ₦12,000. I said profit is ₦180,000 − ₦110,000 − ₦12,000 = ₦58,000.

Think of a mama-put who runs a drinks cooler beside her food. On Monday morning she already had some crates of drinks from last week. She bought more during the week, and on Saturday night some bottles were still in the cooler. The drinks she actually SOLD — were they only the ones she bought this week?
No — she sold some of last week's stock too, and the ones left in the cooler weren't sold.
So the bar trading account works exactly like a trading account. What is the cost of bar sales, using opening stock, purchases and closing stock?
Well done. Now, when you prepare the club's main income and expenditure account, do you bring in the ₦180,000 bar sales, or only this ₦63,000? Why?

examples.correct_understanding: Cost of bar sales = ₦15,000 + ₦110,000 − ₦20,000 = ₦105,000; bar gross profit = ₦180,000 − ₦105,000 = ₦75,000; less bar wages ₦12,000 gives bar profit of ₦63,000, which is transferred to the income and expenditure account as income.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bar trading account
examples.student_opening: In the income and expenditure account I put bar sales on the income side and bar purchases on the expenditure side. Is that okay since they are all club activities?
examples.misconception: Student lists bar sales as income in the income and expenditure account and bar purchases as expenditure, instead of transferring only the bar profit.

turns.text: In the income and expenditure account I put bar sales on the income side and bar purchases on the expenditure side. Is that okay since they are all club activities?

Think of a church harvest bazaar. The harvest committee sells food and drinks, buys ingredients, pays helpers, and at the end announces to the congregation 'the bazaar raised ₦X'. When the church secretary writes the annual report, does she list every tray of jollof sold, or just what the bazaar raised?
Just what the bazaar raised. The details are in the committee's own record.

Good. The bar in a club is like that bazaar — a trading activity inside a non-trading organisation. So where do the detailed bar sales, purchases and stock go first, and what single figure moves across to the income and expenditure account?
They go into a separate bar trading account first, and only the bar profit (or loss) goes to the income and expenditure account.
Exactly. And if the bar made a loss instead, which side of the income and expenditure account would that figure appear on?

examples.correct_understanding: Trading activities of a club (e.g. a bar or canteen) are shown in a separate bar trading account; only the resulting bar profit is transferred to the income side of the income and expenditure account (a bar loss would appear on the expenditure side).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, capital and revenue expenditure in clubs
