examples.student_opening: The town union bought canopies and plastic chairs for ₦120,000 this year. It's in the receipts and payments account as a payment, so I also put ₦120,000 as expenditure in the income and expenditure account.
examples.misconception: Student includes the full cost of new equipment as expenditure in the income and expenditure account because it appears in the receipts and payments account.

turns.text: The town union bought canopies and plastic chairs for ₦120,000 this year. It's in the receipts and payments account as a payment, so I also put ₦120,000 as expenditure in the income and expenditure account.
The union will rent out these chairs for burials and weddings for maybe ten years. If you charge the full cost in one year, how would this year's result look compared with the next nine years?
This year would look like a big deficit, and the next years would look better than they really are.
So is the purchase of the chairs capital expenditure or revenue expenditure? And which statement is the right home for a capital item: the income and expenditure account or the balance sheet?
It's capital expenditure, so the chairs go to the balance sheet as a non-current asset. Only the depreciation goes to the income and expenditure account.
That's it. If the union depreciates the chairs at 10% per annum on cost, what charge would you show this year, and at what value would the chairs appear in the balance sheet?

examples.correct_understanding: Purchase of chairs (₦120,000) is capital expenditure: it appears in the receipts and payments account (cash was paid) and as a non-current asset in the balance sheet, but only the depreciation (e.g. 10% = ₦12,000) is charged in the income and expenditure account; net book value would be ₦108,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, depreciation in club accounts
examples.student_opening: The cooperative thrift society's canopies cost ₦200,000, depreciated at 10% straight line. I put depreciation in the receipts and payments account but my friend says it doesn't go there. Who is right?
examples.misconception: Student expects depreciation to appear in the receipts and payments account because it is an expense.

turns.text: The cooperative thrift society's canopies cost ₦200,000, depreciated at 10% straight line. I put depreciation in the receipts and payments account but my friend says it doesn't go there. Who is right?
Think of your cooperative's cash box. When the canopies get one year older and a bit more worn out, does any money leave the box on the 31st of December because of that wear?
No, no money leaves. They just get older.
And the receipts and payments account records only what? So will depreciation show there, and which statement WILL show it?
Only actual cash movements. So depreciation isn't in the receipts and payments account; it goes in the income and expenditure account as an expense. My friend is right.
Good. Now calculate the depreciation charge for the year, and tell me what happens to the canopies' value in the balance sheet.

examples.correct_understanding: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so it never appears in the receipts and payments account; it is charged in the income and expenditure account. At 10% of ₦200,000, the charge is ₦20,000 and the canopies appear in the balance sheet at ₦180,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, donations and legacies
examples.student_opening: Our old students' association received ₦15,000 general donation from a member, and ₦500,000 from a big man specifically to build the new school library. I put ₦515,000 as income in the income and expenditure account. Is that correct?
examples.misconception: Student treats every donation as ordinary income for the year, including a large donation given specifically for a building project.

turns.text: Our old students' association received ₦15,000 general donation from a member, and ₦500,000 from a big man specifically to build the new school library. I put ₦515,000 as income in the income and expenditure account. Is that correct?

Imagine an uncle gives your family ₦5,000 for the week's soup, and another uncle gives ₦500,000 and says 'this is ONLY for roofing the family house'. Would your mother mix both into the kitchen purse for normal spending?
No! The roofing money will be kept separate. It's not for normal spending.

So for the association, which donation behaves like regular income for running the year, and which one is really a capital receipt tied to a specific purpose? Where might the second one go instead of the income and expenditure account?
The ₦15,000 is normal income. The ₦500,000 should go straight to the accumulated fund, or to a special library fund, in the balance sheet.

Well reasoned. If you put the ₦500,000 in the income and expenditure account, what would happen to the surplus figure, and why would that mislead members about how well the association ran its normal activities?

examples.correct_understanding: Small general donations are revenue income in the income and expenditure account. Large donations or legacies, or those given for a specific capital purpose (e.g. a library building fund), are capitalised — credited to the accumulated fund or a special fund in the balance sheet — unless the question instructs otherwise.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, entrance fees
examples.student_opening: The social club collected ₦30,000 as entrance fees from new members. One textbook adds it to the accumulated fund, another puts it in income and expenditure. Which one will WAEC accept?
examples.misconception: Student is unaware that the treatment of entrance fees depends on the question's instruction and treats them inconsistently.

turns.text: The social club collected ₦30,000 as entrance fees from new members. One textbook adds it to the accumulated fund, another puts it in income and expenditure. Which one will WAEC accept?
Think of joining an Esusu group. You pay a one-off joining fee once in your life, then monthly contributions after. Is the joining fee something that recurs every year like dues, or a one-time thing?
A one-time thing. You only join once.

That one-off nature is exactly why some accountants capitalise entrance fees (to the accumulated fund), while others treat them as income because new members join every year. So when a question includes entrance fees, what should be the FIRST thing you look for in the question before deciding?
Look for an instruction, like 'entrance fees are to be capitalised' or 'treated as income'.
Yes. And if the question is silent, it's safest to state your treatment as a note in your answer. Why would writing that note protect your marks?

examples.correct_understanding: Entrance fees may be capitalised (credited to the accumulated fund) or treated as revenue income in the income and expenditure account; students must follow the question's instruction and, if none is given, state the assumption they have made.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accumulated fund
examples.student_opening: The PTA fund had an accumulated fund of ₦250,000 at the start of the year and the income and expenditure account shows a surplus of ₦38,000. What do I do with the surplus in the balance sheet?
examples.misconception: Student does not know how the surplus for the year affects the accumulated fund.

turns.text: The PTA fund had an accumulated fund of ₦250,000 at the start of the year and the income and expenditure account shows a surplus of ₦38,000. What do I do with the surplus in the balance sheet?
Think of your family's savings box. If it held some money in January, and during the year the family saved an extra amount after all spending, what happens to the savings box by December?
It increases by the extra amount saved.
The accumulated fund is the PTA's 'savings box' — what members' contributions have built up over the years. So what would the closing accumulated fund be?
Correct. In a sole trader's balance sheet, which item does the accumulated fund replace, and what item do clubs NOT have that traders deduct from capital?

examples.correct_understanding: Closing accumulated fund = opening accumulated fund ₦250,000 + surplus ₦38,000 = ₦288,000. It replaces capital in a club balance sheet; clubs have no drawings.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accumulated fund
examples.student_opening: Accumulated fund at start ₦180,000. The income and expenditure account shows a DEFICIT of ₦22,000. So the closing fund is ₦202,000, abi?
examples.misconception: Student adds a deficit to the accumulated fund as if it were a surplus.

turns.text: Accumulated fund at start ₦180,000. The income and expenditure account shows a DEFICIT of ₦22,000. So the closing fund is ₦202,000, abi?
Suppose your town union's purse had some money in January, and during the year the union spent more on the chief's reception than it collected in levies. Did the purse get fuller or emptier?
I don't understand. Deficit or surplus, isn't it all just added at the end? Tell me the correct thing.

No problem, let's make it concrete. A deficit means expenditure was MORE than income — the union used up some of its old savings to cover the gap. So the deficit REDUCES the fund. Try the calculation again using subtraction: ₦180,000 minus the deficit.
Hmm, so ₦180,000 − ₦22,000? I'm not sure I believe it.

Let's check it the long way. Suppose income was ₦100,000 and expenditure ₦122,000 — that's a deficit of ₦22,000. The union had to take ₦22,000 from its savings to pay the extra bills. So the accumulated fund falls: ₦180,000 − ₦22,000 = ₦158,000. A surplus is added to the fund; a deficit is deducted.

examples.correct_understanding: A deficit reduces the accumulated fund: ₦180,000 − ₦22,000 = ₦158,000. Only a surplus is added.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, income and expenditure account
examples.student_opening: Prepare the income and expenditure account: subscriptions ₦97,000, bar profit ₦40,000, donations ₦15,000, rent ₦36,000, electricity ₦18,000, depreciation ₦20,000, secretary's honorarium ₦30,000. I don't even know which side is which.
examples.misconception: Student mixes income and expenditure items on the wrong sides and cannot arrive at the surplus.

turns.text: Prepare the income and expenditure account: subscriptions ₦97,000, bar profit ₦40,000, donations ₦15,000, rent ₦36,000, electricity ₦18,000, depreciation ₦20,000, secretary's honorarium ₦30,000. I don't even know which side is which.

Picture the social club's end-of-year meeting. The treasurer reads out 'money we earned this year' first, then 'what it cost us to run the club', and finally tells members whether they are better or worse off. Which of your items are 'money we earned'?
Subscriptions, donations... I'm not sure about bar profit. Honestly, just show me the whole thing, I'm tired.

Fair enough, you're closer than you think. Bar profit is ALSO earned income — it's the net result of the bar. So income = subscriptions + bar profit + donations. Everything else (rent, electricity, depreciation, honorarium) is expenditure. Add up the income group first. What do you get?
₦152,000. But I still don't know how to set it out or what comes after.

Here it is in ledger form — expenditure on the debit side, income on the credit side, and the surplus is the balancing figure:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 31 Dec | Rent | 36,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Electricity | 18,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Depreciation of equipment | 20,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Secretary's honorarium | 30,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Subscriptions |  | 97,000 |
| 31 Dec | Bar profit |  | 40,000 |
| 31 Dec | Donations |  | 15,000 |
| 31 Dec | Surplus to accumulated fund | 48,000 |  |
|  | Total | 152,000 | 152,000 |
Total income ₦152,000 − total expenditure ₦104,000 = surplus ₦48,000, which is added to the accumulated fund.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accruals in club accounts
examples.student_opening: The receipts and payments account shows rent paid ₦40,000. This includes ₦8,000 owed from last year. At year end, ₦6,000 rent is still owing. The rent for the income and expenditure account is ₦40,000, right?
examples.misconception: Student uses rent paid (from the receipts and payments account) as the rent expense without adjusting for opening and closing accruals.

turns.text: The receipts and payments account shows rent paid ₦40,000. This includes ₦8,000 owed from last year. At year end, ₦6,000 rent is still owing. The rent for the income and expenditure account is ₦40,000, right?

Think of an okada rider who pays his owner weekly. In January he paid off ₦8,000 he owed from December, and at the end of this year he still owes the last ₦6,000. If you want to know what the bike hire for THIS year really cost him, is it just the total cash he handed over?
No. Some of the cash was for last year, and some of this year's cost hasn't been paid.
Right. So which of the two figures, ₦8,000 and ₦6,000, do you remove from ₦40,000, and which do you add?
Remove the ₦8,000 for last year, add the ₦6,000 still owing. ₦40,000 − ₦8,000 + ₦6,000 = ₦38,000.
Exactly. And where does the ₦6,000 owing appear in the club's balance sheet?

examples.correct_understanding: Rent expense = paid ₦40,000 − opening accrual ₦8,000 + closing accrual ₦6,000 = ₦38,000. The ₦6,000 is shown as a current liability (accrued expense).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, prepayments in club accounts
examples.student_opening: Insurance paid during the year ₦24,000, of which ₦6,000 covers next year. At the start of the year, ₦4,000 had been prepaid from last year. I got insurance expense = ₦24,000 − ₦6,000 = ₦18,000.
examples.misconception: Student ignores the opening prepayment and only deducts the closing prepayment.

turns.text: Insurance paid during the year ₦24,000, of which ₦6,000 covers next year. At the start of the year, ₦4,000 had been prepaid from last year. I got insurance expense = ₦24,000 − ₦6,000 = ₦18,000.
Think of a POS agent who paid ahead for her kiosk space. At the start of this year she had already paid ₦4,000 last year for part of THIS year's space. Did she use that space this year?
Yes, she used it this year even though she paid last year.
So the benefit of that opening prepayment is consumed this year. Should it be part of this year's expense or not? Adjust your figure.
Correct. And the ₦6,000 for next year — which side of the balance sheet does it sit on, and under what heading?

examples.correct_understanding: Insurance expense = paid ₦24,000 − closing prepayment ₦6,000 + opening prepayment ₦4,000 = ₦22,000. The closing prepayment of ₦6,000 is a current asset.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, receipts and payments account
examples.student_opening: Our church harvest committee's receipts and payments account ended with a 'deficit of ₦12,000'. Is that the right word?
examples.misconception: Student thinks the receipts and payments account can show a deficit like the income and expenditure account.

turns.text: Our church harvest committee's receipts and payments account ended with a 'deficit of ₦12,000'. Is that the right word?
The receipts and payments account is really the treasurer's cash box summary. If you open a cash box at the end of the year, can it contain MINUS ₦12,000 in notes?
No, a box can't have negative money. But the bank account can be overdrawn.

Good point. So the closing figure in a receipts and payments account is a balance of cash or bank — it may be cash in hand or a bank overdraft. Which statement is the one that can show a surplus or deficit?
The income and expenditure account. So in the receipts and payments account I should call it a balance c/d, or a bank overdraft if it's negative.
Exactly. So what kind of account is the receipts and payments account — a real account like cash, or a nominal account like profit and loss?

examples.correct_understanding: The receipts and payments account is a real (cash) account summarising the cash book; its closing figure is a cash/bank balance (or bank overdraft), never a surplus or deficit. Surplus/deficit belongs to the income and expenditure account, which is a nominal account.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, disposal of assets in club accounts
examples.student_opening: The social club sold its old generator for ₦35,000. Its book value was ₦30,000. I put ₦35,000 as income in the income and expenditure account. My teacher said no, but it IS money received!
examples.misconception: Student puts the full sale proceeds of an old asset in the income and expenditure account as income.

turns.text: The social club sold its old generator for ₦35,000. Its book value was ₦30,000. I put ₦35,000 as income in the income and expenditure account. My teacher said no, but it IS money received!

Suppose a trader at Alaba sells an old deep freezer in his shop for ₦35,000. Before selling, his records valued it at ₦30,000. Did the sale make him ₦35,000 richer, or did he just swap the freezer for cash?
I don't know. He received the money, so he is richer. I'm not getting this, just tell me.

Okay, let's go one step at a time. Before the sale, he owned a freezer worth ₦30,000. After the sale, he owns cash of ₦35,000 and no freezer. So his total wealth changed by only the DIFFERENCE between the two. The ₦35,000 goes into the receipts and payments account because it is cash. What goes into the income and expenditure account is only that difference. What is it?
So it's not the full amount... but I'm still not sure what the difference is called or which side.

Here it is fully: proceeds ₦35,000 − book value ₦30,000 = ₦5,000. Because proceeds exceed book value, it is a profit (gain) on disposal of ₦5,000, shown on the income side of the income and expenditure account. The full ₦35,000 appears only as a receipt in the receipts and payments account, and the generator is removed from the balance sheet.

examples.correct_understanding: Only the gain on disposal (₦35,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦5,000) is income in the income and expenditure account; the full ₦35,000 proceeds appear in the receipts and payments account.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, special events in club accounts
examples.student_opening: Our church harvest bazaar received ₦85,000 and spent ₦30,000 on food and decorations. How do I show it in the income and expenditure account?
examples.misconception: Student shows bazaar receipts as income and bazaar expenses separately rather than netting them.

turns.text: Our church harvest bazaar received ₦85,000 and spent ₦30,000 on food and decorations. How do I show it in the income and expenditure account?
When the pastor announces the bazaar result on Sunday, does he say 'we sold ₦85,000 and spent ₦30,000', or does he just announce how much the bazaar brought in for the church?
He usually says the bazaar raised a certain amount — after expenses.
Clubs often do the same in the income and expenditure account — they show the event's net figure on the income side, with the details as a working. What would that net figure be here?
Good. And if the bazaar expenses had been bigger than the receipts, where would the net figure appear then?

examples.correct_understanding: Net proceeds from the bazaar = ₦85,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦55,000, shown as income in the income and expenditure account (a net loss would be shown as expenditure).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, accumulated fund
examples.student_opening: The question says 'calculate the accumulated fund at 1 January'. It's not given anywhere! Items: clubhouse ₦500,000, furniture ₦80,000, bar stock ₦12,000, bank ₦35,000, subscriptions in arrears ₦3,000, subscriptions in advance ₦2,000, wages accrued ₦8,000, bar creditors ₦10,000.
examples.misconception: Student does not know how to compute the opening accumulated fund when it is not given.

turns.text: The question says 'calculate the accumulated fund at 1 January'. It's not given anywhere! Items: clubhouse ₦500,000, furniture ₦80,000, bar stock ₦12,000, bank ₦35,000, subscriptions in arrears ₦3,000, subscriptions in advance ₦2,000, wages accrued ₦8,000, bar creditors ₦10,000.

Think of a town union being handed over to a new executive. The old executive lists everything the union owns, and everything it owes. How would the new executive know what the union is really 'worth' on handover day?
I don't know... add everything? This is where I always fall. Please just do it.

It's okay, you're nearly there. The worth is what the union OWNS minus what it OWES. Owns: clubhouse, furniture, bar stock, bank, and subscriptions in arrears (members owe the club). Owes: subscriptions in advance, wages accrued, bar creditors. Add the 'owns' list first — what is it?
₦630,000? Then I don't know what next.

Yes, assets = ₦630,000. Liabilities = ₦2,000 + ₦8,000 + ₦10,000 = ₦20,000. Accumulated fund at 1 January = ₦630,000 − ₦20,000 = ₦610,000. This is really an opening statement of affairs for the club — the same idea as capital = assets − liabilities.

examples.correct_understanding: Opening accumulated fund = total assets ₦630,000 − total liabilities ₦20,000 = ₦610,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, bar trading account
examples.student_opening: Cash paid to bar suppliers was ₦90,000. Bar creditors were ₦8,000 at the start and ₦11,000 at the end. For the bar trading account I put purchases ₦90,000.
examples.misconception: Student uses cash paid to bar suppliers as bar purchases without adjusting for opening and closing bar creditors.

turns.text: Cash paid to bar suppliers was ₦90,000. Bar creditors were ₦8,000 at the start and ₦11,000 at the end. For the bar trading account I put purchases ₦90,000.

Picture the club buying crates of drinks on credit from a distributor at Idumota. Some of the cash paid this year cleared LAST year's crates, and some of this year's crates haven't been paid for yet. Is the cash paid equal to the crates bought this year?
No. I need to remove the old debt that was paid and add what's still owed for this year's crates.
Right. Do it with the three figures. What are this year's bar purchases?
Correct. Notice this is the same logic as a total creditors account in incomplete records. Why do you think clubs so often need this kind of reconstruction?

examples.correct_understanding: Bar purchases = cash paid ₦90,000 − opening creditors ₦8,000 + closing creditors ₦11,000 = ₦93,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, nature of non-profit organisations
examples.student_opening: In the social club balance sheet, where do I show the members' drawings? And where is the capital?
examples.misconception: Student expects members of a club to have drawings and capital accounts like owners of a business.

turns.text: In the social club balance sheet, where do I show the members' drawings? And where is the capital?
In your old students' association, if an old boy needs money for his own house rent, can he walk to the treasurer and 'draw' from the association's funds like a shop owner taking from his own shop?
No oh! That would be stealing. The money belongs to the association, not to him.
Exactly. So there are no drawings. And since no single person owns the club, what replaces 'capital' in the balance sheet?
The accumulated fund — it belongs to the club as a whole.
Correct. What is the main aim of a club, if not profit — and how does that explain why it uses 'surplus' instead of 'profit'?

examples.correct_understanding: Non-profit organisations have no owners, so there are no drawings or capital accounts; the accumulated fund takes the place of capital, and the organisation exists to provide services to members rather than profit, hence 'surplus/deficit'.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, receipts and payments account
examples.student_opening: The cooperative thrift society: bank at start ₦10,000, receipts ₦60,000, payments ₦78,000. I got −₦8,000 and I think I made a mistake because money can't be negative.
examples.misconception: Student does not recognise that a negative closing bank balance in the receipts and payments account is an overdraft, a liability.

turns.text: The cooperative thrift society: bank at start ₦10,000, receipts ₦60,000, payments ₦78,000. I got −₦8,000 and I think I made a mistake because money can't be negative.

Think of a POS agent whose bank allows her to go below zero for a short time so she can still pay customers. At the end of the day, if she has paid out more than she had, what does she now have with the bank — money, or a debt?
A debt. The bank has lent her the difference.
So your −₦8,000 isn't necessarily a mistake. How would you describe it in words in the receipts and payments account, and where does it go in the balance sheet?
It's a bank overdraft of ₦8,000, and it goes under current liabilities.
Correct. In the receipts and payments account, the overdraft would appear as the balancing figure on which side — the receipts side or the payments side?

examples.correct_understanding: Closing bank = ₦10,000 + ₦60,000 − ₦78,000 = −₦8,000, i.e. a bank overdraft of ₦8,000, shown as a current liability; in the receipts and payments account it is the balancing figure on the receipts (debit) side.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, subscriptions account
examples.student_opening:
Here is my subscriptions account. ₦50,000 was received during the year and ₦4,000 of it was for next year. There were no arrears.
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 50,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 50,000 |  |
|  | Total | 50,000 | 50,000 |
It balances, so it must be right?
examples.misconception: Student transfers all subscriptions received to the income and expenditure account, including subscriptions paid in advance for next year.

turns.text:
Here is my subscriptions account. ₦50,000 was received during the year and ₦4,000 of it was for next year. There were no arrears.
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 50,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 50,000 |  |
|  | Total | 50,000 | 50,000 |
It balances, so it must be right?

A tailor collects money for Christmas outfits in November, including deposits for Easter outfits she hasn't started sewing. If she tells her husband 'I earned all of this this season', is she telling the full truth?
No — the Easter money is for work she hasn't done. She'd still owe those customers.
So in your account, which part of the ₦50,000 should NOT go to income and expenditure this year, and how would you carry it forward?
The ₦4,000 for next year. I'll carry it down as a balance c/d, so income is ₦46,000.

That's it — your corrected account would look like this:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 50,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 46,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in advance) | 4,000 |  |
|  | Total | 50,000 | 50,000 |
A balanced account isn't proof of correctness. When you bring the ₦4,000 down next year, will it be a debit or a credit balance b/d, and what does that tell you about its nature?

examples.correct_understanding: Only ₦46,000 is subscription income; the ₦4,000 received for next year is carried down as a credit balance (subscriptions in advance), a current liability.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, consumables in club accounts
examples.student_opening: School PTA: stationery stock at start ₦3,000, stationery bought ₦12,000, stationery left at end ₦2,500. What is the stationery expense? I wrote ₦12,000.
examples.misconception: Student uses stationery purchased as the expense figure, ignoring opening and closing stocks of stationery.

turns.text: School PTA: stationery stock at start ₦3,000, stationery bought ₦12,000, stationery left at end ₦2,500. What is the stationery expense? I wrote ₦12,000.
Think of the exercise books your mum buys at the start of term. If you still had some from last term, and some new ones are unused at the end of this term, how many did you actually USE this term?
The old ones plus the new ones, minus the unused ones at the end.
Apply that to the PTA's stationery. What figure do you get?
Correct. And the ₦2,500 unused stationery — where would it appear in the PTA's balance sheet?

examples.correct_understanding: Stationery used = opening stock ₦3,000 + purchases ₦12,000 − closing stock ₦2,500 = ₦12,500; the closing stock of ₦2,500 is a current asset.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, receipts and payments vs income and expenditure
examples.student_opening: Which of these go in receipts and payments ONLY, and which go in income and expenditure ONLY: opening cash balance, purchase of a canopy, subscriptions received for last year, depreciation of chairs?
examples.misconception: Student assumes every item in the receipts and payments account must also appear in the income and expenditure account.

turns.text: Which of these go in receipts and payments ONLY, and which go in income and expenditure ONLY: opening cash balance, purchase of a canopy, subscriptions received for last year, depreciation of chairs?

Use the cash box test from the town union treasurer: for each item, ask 'did cash physically move this year?' Then use the fairness test: 'is this truly THIS year's income or expense?' Start with the opening cash balance — does it pass the cash box test, the fairness test, or both?
It's cash, so it's in receipts and payments. But it's not income of this year, so not in income and expenditure.
Good. Now run the canopy, last year's subscriptions and depreciation through the same two tests.

Canopy: cash moved, but it's capital, so receipts and payments only. Last year's subscriptions: cash received, but last year's income, so receipts and payments only. Depreciation: no cash, but it is this year's expense, so income and expenditure only.
All four correct. Can you think of an item that would appear in BOTH statements, and one that would appear in NEITHER but only in the balance sheet?

examples.correct_understanding: Opening cash balance, purchase of a canopy (capital) and subscriptions received for a previous year appear only in the receipts and payments account; depreciation appears only in the income and expenditure account. Items like this year's subscriptions received appear in both.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, meaning of incomplete records
examples.student_opening: My aunty sells food by the roadside. She has no ledger, only a cash tin and a small notebook where she writes who owes her. My teacher says that's 'incomplete records'. How can anyone calculate her profit like that?
examples.misconception: Student thinks a trader who does not keep full double-entry books has no records at all and profit cannot be found.

turns.text: My aunty sells food by the roadside. She has no ledger, only a cash tin and a small notebook where she writes who owes her. My teacher says that's 'incomplete records'. How can anyone calculate her profit like that?

Good question. Even without a ledger, suppose you visited your aunty's stall today and again one year from now, and each time you counted everything she owns — pots, stock of rice, cash in the tin, money customers owe her — and subtracted what she owes her suppliers. What would comparing those two counts tell you?
Whether she is richer or poorer than last year.

Exactly. So 'incomplete records' doesn't mean NO records — it means records that are not kept under full double entry. What do you think accountants call the single-entry method of finding the business's worth on a given date by listing assets and liabilities?
A statement of affairs? It shows capital = assets minus liabilities.
Right. And her cash tin and debtors notebook are still very useful — which figures could you rebuild from them if you wanted a full trading account instead of just the capital comparison?

examples.correct_understanding: Incomplete records (single entry) are records not kept on the full double-entry system. Profit can still be found by comparing capital in opening and closing statements of affairs (capital = assets − liabilities), or by reconstructing sales, purchases and expenses from cash records to prepare final accounts.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, statement of affairs
examples.student_opening: Mama Chidi's provisions stall on 31 December: stall fittings ₦40,000, stock ₦65,000, debtors ₦12,000, cash ₦8,000, creditors ₦20,000. I added all to get capital of ₦145,000.
examples.misconception: Student adds creditors to assets when computing capital in a statement of affairs.

turns.text: Mama Chidi's provisions stall on 31 December: stall fittings ₦40,000, stock ₦65,000, debtors ₦12,000, cash ₦8,000, creditors ₦20,000. I added all to get capital of ₦145,000.
If Mama Chidi closed her stall today, sold everything, collected from customers who owe her, and then paid her own suppliers — would the suppliers' money be hers to keep?
No, she has to pay them. That money is not hers.
So in the statement of affairs, what do you do with the creditors figure, and what is her true capital?
Good. This is the same accounting equation as in any balance sheet. Why do you think it's called a 'statement of affairs' rather than a balance sheet when records are incomplete?

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, profit from capital comparison
examples.student_opening: Opening capital ₦120,000, closing capital ₦175,000, drawings ₦30,000, additional capital introduced ₦10,000. I said profit = ₦175,000 − ₦120,000 = ₦55,000.
examples.misconception: Student takes the increase in capital as profit without adjusting for drawings and additional capital introduced.

turns.text: Opening capital ₦120,000, closing capital ₦175,000, drawings ₦30,000, additional capital introduced ₦10,000. I said profit = ₦175,000 − ₦120,000 = ₦55,000.

Think of a POS agent whose float grew from ₦120,000 to ₦175,000 over the year. During the year she took ₦30,000 for her children's school fees, and her husband also put ₦10,000 into the float. Is all of the growth in the float from her business earnings?
Ehn... I don't know how to handle both of them together. Just tell me the formula.

No wahala. Take them one at a time. The ₦30,000 she took out was profit she had ALREADY earned and then removed — so the ₦55,000 growth is too small; you add drawings back. The ₦10,000 from her husband isn't earnings at all — so you remove it. Try ₦55,000 + ₦30,000 − ₦10,000.
So I add one and subtract the other... I'm still confusing myself which is which.

Let's lay it out:
Closing capital ₦175,000
Less opening capital ₦120,000 → increase ₦55,000
Add drawings ₦30,000 (profit taken out) → ₦85,000
Less capital introduced ₦10,000 (not profit) → ₦75,000
Net profit = ₦75,000. The formula is: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings − capital introduced.

examples.correct_understanding: Net profit = closing capital ₦175,000 − opening capital ₦120,000 + drawings ₦30,000 − capital introduced ₦10,000 = ₦75,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, profit from capital comparison
examples.student_opening: When finding profit from capital, why do we ADD drawings? Drawings reduce capital, so I'd subtract them.
examples.misconception: Student thinks drawings should be subtracted when finding profit from capital changes because drawings reduce capital.

turns.text: When finding profit from capital, why do we ADD drawings? Drawings reduce capital, so I'd subtract them.

Picture a suya seller who earned ₦10,000 profit this week but spent ₦4,000 of it on his family's food on Friday. If you count his cash on Saturday, you see only ₦6,000 more than last week. Did he really earn only ₦6,000?
No — he earned ₦10,000. He just spent ₦4,000 of it.
So when the increase in capital looks smaller because drawings were taken out, what must you do to get back to the true profit?
Add the drawings back to the increase in capital.

Exactly. You're right that drawings reduce capital — that's precisely WHY they are added back. Using the same thinking, what would you do with extra money the owner brought in from outside the business?

examples.correct_understanding: Drawings reduce closing capital, so the increase in capital understates profit; drawings must therefore be added back to the change in capital to find the true profit earned.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, profit from capital comparison
examples.student_opening: My teacher said subtract 'capital introduced' when calculating profit from statements of affairs. But the money went into the business, so isn't it part of the business's gain?
examples.misconception: Student treats capital introduced during the year as part of profit.

turns.text: My teacher said subtract 'capital introduced' when calculating profit from statements of affairs. But the money went into the business, so isn't it part of the business's gain?

Suppose an Alaba electronics trader's shop is worth ₦2m in January. In June his uncle gives him ₦500,000 to add to the shop. In December the shop is worth ₦2.5m. Did the trader's buying and selling earn him anything?
No. The shop grew only because of the uncle's money.
So the increase in capital is ₦500,000, but profit from trading is...? And what does that tell you about why capital introduced must be removed?
Zero profit. Capital introduced increases capital without being earned, so we subtract it to avoid overstating profit.
Correct. If a question tells you the trader also won a ₦100,000 lottery and put it in the shop, how would you treat it?

examples.correct_understanding: Capital introduced increases closing capital without being earned from trading, so it must be deducted from the increase in capital to avoid overstating profit.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, profit from capital comparison
examples.student_opening: Opening capital ₦200,000, closing capital ₦185,000, drawings ₦5,000. No new capital. I keep getting a minus figure. I think the question is wrong.
examples.misconception: Student does not recognise that a negative result from the capital comparison formula represents a net loss.

turns.text: Opening capital ₦200,000, closing capital ₦185,000, drawings ₦5,000. No new capital. I keep getting a minus figure. I think the question is wrong.
Imagine a keke owner whose business was worth ₦200,000 in January and only ₦185,000 in December, even though he only took ₦5,000 for himself. Would you say the keke business made money this year?
I don't know. Can profit be negative? Just tell me if the answer is minus.

Good instinct to question it. Think: even after adding back the small ₦5,000 he took, the business is still worth LESS than it started. So it hasn't made a profit — what is the opposite of profit called? Compute ₦185,000 − ₦200,000 + ₦5,000 and name the result.
I get −₦10,000 but I still don't know how to write it.

Here it is: closing capital ₦185,000 − opening capital ₦200,000 = −₦15,000 (a decrease). Add back drawings ₦5,000: −₦15,000 + ₦5,000 = −₦10,000. A negative figure means the business made a NET LOSS of ₦10,000. The question isn't wrong — you'd write 'Net loss for the year ₦10,000'.

examples.correct_understanding: Closing capital ₦185,000 − opening capital ₦200,000 + drawings ₦5,000 = −₦10,000, i.e. a net loss of ₦10,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, total debtors account
examples.student_opening: An Alaba trader's records: cash received from debtors ₦150,000; debtors at start ₦20,000; debtors at end ₦28,000. What are the credit sales? I think it's ₦150,000.
examples.misconception: Student takes cash received from debtors as the credit sales figure.

turns.text: An Alaba trader's records: cash received from debtors ₦150,000; debtors at start ₦20,000; debtors at end ₦28,000. What are the credit sales? I think it's ₦150,000.

The trader keeps a notebook of customers who owe him. At the start of the year some names were already in it. During the year, customers paid him, and at year end some names were still unpaid. Were all the payments he received for goods sold THIS year?
No, some were for last year's debts. And some of this year's sales are still unpaid.
So starting from cash received, which debtors figure do you remove, and which do you add?
Remove opening debtors and add closing debtors: ₦150,000 − ₦20,000 + ₦28,000 = ₦158,000.

Correct. Here's the total debtors account that proves it — credit sales is the balancing figure:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d | 20,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Cash (received from debtors) |  | 150,000 |
| 31 Dec | Credit sales | 158,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d |  | 28,000 |
|  | Total | 178,000 | 178,000 |
If the question also mentioned discounts allowed, which side of this account would they go on?

examples.correct_understanding: Credit sales = cash received from debtors ₦150,000 − opening debtors ₦20,000 + closing debtors ₦28,000 = ₦158,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, reconstructing sales
examples.student_opening: A mama-put owner banked ₦70,000 of her cash takings. Before banking, she used ₦15,000 from the takings to buy firewood and pay her helper. Credit sales (to offices nearby) were ₦60,000. Total sales: I said ₦130,000.
examples.misconception: Student takes only cash sales banked as cash sales, ignoring takings used to pay expenses before banking.

turns.text: A mama-put owner banked ₦70,000 of her cash takings. Before banking, she used ₦15,000 from the takings to buy firewood and pay her helper. Credit sales (to offices nearby) were ₦60,000. Total sales: I said ₦130,000.
Every evening she empties her cash tin. Before going to the bank, she pays the firewood seller from the tin. Did that firewood money come from food she sold?
Yes, it came from her sales. So it's part of the takings.
So what were her total cash sales, and then her total sales including the credit sales?
Correct. And the ₦15,000 — besides adding it to sales, where else must it appear so her expenses aren't understated?

examples.correct_understanding: Cash sales = amount banked ₦70,000 + takings used before banking ₦15,000 = ₦85,000; total sales = ₦85,000 + credit sales ₦60,000 = ₦145,000. The ₦15,000 spent must also be included in expenses.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, total creditors account
examples.student_opening: Paid to creditors ₦110,000; discount received ₦2,000; creditors at start ₦18,000; at end ₦25,000. Find credit purchases. I did ₦110,000 − ₦18,000 + ₦25,000 = ₦117,000 but the answer says ₦119,000. Why?
examples.misconception: Student forgets that discount received also settles creditors and so omits it when reconstructing credit purchases.

turns.text: Paid to creditors ₦110,000; discount received ₦2,000; creditors at start ₦18,000; at end ₦25,000. Find credit purchases. I did ₦110,000 − ₦18,000 + ₦25,000 = ₦117,000 but the answer says ₦119,000. Why?
A trader owed a Kano grain supplier. She paid him cash, and because she paid early, he said 'forget the last ₦2,000'. After that, does she still owe the ₦2,000?
I don't understand what discount has to do with purchases. Abeg just explain.

Sure. The debt was cleared in TWO ways: ₦110,000 by cash AND ₦2,000 by discount. Both reduce what she owes, so both go on the debit side of the creditors account. That means the total goods bought on credit must cover both. Add ₦2,000 to your working and see what you get.
So I add it... but I'm still not sure how it all fits.

Here's the total creditors account; credit purchases is the balancing figure:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 31 Dec | Bank (paid to creditors) | 110,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Discount received | 2,000 |  |
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d |  | 18,000 |
| 31 Dec | Credit purchases |  | 119,000 |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d | 25,000 |  |
|  | Total | 137,000 | 137,000 |
Working: ₦110,000 + ₦2,000 + ₦25,000 − ₦18,000 = ₦119,000. Your ₦117,000 missed the ₦2,000 of debt settled by discount.

examples.correct_understanding: Credit purchases = cash paid ₦110,000 + discount received ₦2,000 + closing creditors ₦25,000 − opening creditors ₦18,000 = ₦119,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, total debtors account
examples.student_opening: Cash from debtors ₦95,000, discounts allowed ₦3,000, bad debts written off ₦2,000, opening debtors ₦15,000, closing debtors ₦19,000. Find credit sales.
examples.misconception: Student forgets that discounts allowed and bad debts also reduce debtors, so omits them when reconstructing credit sales.

turns.text: Cash from debtors ₦95,000, discounts allowed ₦3,000, bad debts written off ₦2,000, opening debtors ₦15,000, closing debtors ₦19,000. Find credit sales.

Think of a tailor's credit customers. Some paid in cash, some got a small 'discount' for paying early, and one customer relocated to Abuja and never paid. In all three cases, did the names leave the tailor's 'owing' notebook?
Yes — all of them cleared their debt one way or another.
So in the total debtors account, what are ALL the credit-side items that cleared debts? Use them with the opening and closing balances to find credit sales.
Credit side: cash ₦95,000, discount ₦3,000, bad debts ₦2,000, closing debtors ₦19,000. Debit side: opening ₦15,000 + credit sales. So credit sales = ₦119,000 − ₦15,000 = ₦104,000.
Excellent. Which of those items — discount allowed or bad debts — also needs to appear as an expense in the profit and loss account?

examples.correct_understanding: Credit sales = ₦95,000 + ₦3,000 + ₦2,000 + ₦19,000 − ₦15,000 = ₦104,000; discounts allowed and bad debts both appear as expenses in the profit and loss account.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, missing figures in cash account
examples.student_opening: A mama-put's cash tin: ₦5,000 at start, cash sales ₦240,000, paid for foodstuff ₦150,000, paid expenses ₦30,000, ₦7,000 at year end. She says she 'took some money for home' but didn't write it down. How do I find it?
examples.misconception: Student does not realise that an unrecorded balancing figure in the cash account can represent the owner's drawings.

turns.text: A mama-put's cash tin: ₦5,000 at start, cash sales ₦240,000, paid for foodstuff ₦150,000, paid expenses ₦30,000, ₦7,000 at year end. She says she 'took some money for home' but didn't write it down. How do I find it?

Think of the cash tin as a bucket of water. You know how much was in it at the start, how much you poured in, how much you used for cooking and washing, and how much is left. If the numbers don't add up, what does that tell you?
That some water went somewhere else. But I don't know how to turn that into drawings. Please just show me.

You're right that some 'went somewhere else' — that's the missing drawings. Step one: what cash was AVAILABLE? That's opening cash + sales: ₦5,000 + ₦240,000. Then subtract everything recorded as leaving or remaining: purchases, expenses and closing cash. The leftover gap is what she took home.
Available is ₦245,000... and then I subtract... I'm getting lost in the steps.

Let's do it line by line:
Cash available: ₦5,000 + ₦240,000 = ₦245,000
Less foodstuff ₦150,000 → ₦95,000
Less expenses ₦30,000 → ₦65,000
Less closing cash ₦7,000 → ₦58,000
The unexplained ₦58,000 is her drawings — the balancing figure in the cash account.

examples.correct_understanding: Drawings = opening cash ₦5,000 + cash sales ₦240,000 − purchases ₦150,000 − expenses ₦30,000 − closing cash ₦7,000 = ₦58,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, mark-up
examples.student_opening: Cost of goods sold was ₦80,000. The trader adds 25% mark-up. How do I find sales?
examples.misconception: Student applies the mark-up percentage to an unknown sales figure instead of to cost of sales.

turns.text: Cost of goods sold was ₦80,000. The trader adds 25% mark-up. How do I find sales?
When a Balogun market trader buys a bundle of fabric and 'adds 25% on top', is she adding 25% of what she PAID for it, or 25% of what she'll SELL it for?
25% of what she paid for it — that's the cost.
So mark-up is based on cost. What is the gross profit here, and then what are the sales?
Correct. What would the gross profit be as a percentage of SALES — and what is that percentage called?

examples.correct_understanding: Mark-up is a percentage of cost: gross profit = 25% × ₦80,000 = ₦20,000; sales = ₦80,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦100,000 (gross margin = 20% of sales).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, gross margin
examples.student_opening: Sales were ₦150,000 and the gross margin is 20%. I found cost of sales as ₦150,000 ÷ 1.2 = ₦125,000. Correct?
examples.misconception: Student applies the margin percentage to cost instead of to sales.

turns.text: Sales were ₦150,000 and the gross margin is 20%. I found cost of sales as ₦150,000 ÷ 1.2 = ₦125,000. Correct?
When an okada owner says 'out of every ₦100 my rider brings back, I keep ₦20 as my profit', is he talking about a share of what he SELLS (the takings) or of his cost?
A share of the takings — of the sales.
Margin works exactly like that — it's a percentage of sales. So what is the gross profit, and then the cost of sales?
Correct. Your ₦125,000 would be right if 20% were a mark-up on cost. So when should you divide by 1.2 — margin or mark-up questions?

examples.correct_understanding: Margin is based on sales: gross profit = 20% × ₦150,000 = ₦30,000; cost of sales = ₦150,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦120,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, mark-up and margin conversion
examples.student_opening: Sales ₦200,000, mark-up on cost 25%. I said gross profit = 25% × ₦200,000 = ₦50,000. My teacher said wrong. I don't see why!
examples.misconception: Student applies a mark-up percentage directly to sales, overstating gross profit.

turns.text: Sales ₦200,000, mark-up on cost 25%. I said gross profit = 25% × ₦200,000 = ₦50,000. My teacher said wrong. I don't see why!
Think of a pure water seller who buys a bag for ₦400 and adds 25% mark-up. What does she sell it for, and what fraction of that SELLING price is her profit?
She sells for ₦500. Profit is ₦100... I don't know how that helps. Please just tell me the rule.

Look carefully at her numbers: profit ₦100 is 25% of cost (₦400) but only ₦100/₦500 = 20% of the selling price. So a 25% mark-up equals a 20% margin. Since you're given SALES, which percentage should you apply to it?
The 20%? But I'm not sure how that converts in general.

Here's the general rule: mark-up of a/b on cost → margin of a/(a+b) on sales. 25% = 1/4 → margin = 1/(1+4) = 1/5 = 20%. So gross profit = 20% × ₦200,000 = ₦40,000, and cost of sales = ₦160,000. Check: 25% × ₦160,000 = ₦40,000. Your ₦50,000 applied the cost-based percentage to sales.

examples.correct_understanding: A 25% mark-up equals a 20% margin (1/4 → 1/5). Gross profit = 20% × ₦200,000 = ₦40,000; cost of sales = ₦160,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, stock lost by fire or theft
examples.student_opening: A fire burnt part of a shop at Onitsha main market. Opening stock ₦30,000, purchases ₦120,000, sales ₦160,000, gross margin 25%. Stock salvaged ₦12,000. How do I find the stock lost?
examples.misconception: Student subtracts salvaged stock from purchases directly and does not use the gross margin to estimate cost of goods sold.

turns.text: A fire burnt part of a shop at Onitsha main market. Opening stock ₦30,000, purchases ₦120,000, sales ₦160,000, gross margin 25%. Stock salvaged ₦12,000. How do I find the stock lost?
Think of it as working out what SHOULD have been on the shelves just before the fire. You know what was there at the start and what came in. What do you need to subtract to find what should remain?
What went out — the goods sold. But at cost, not selling price.
Right. Sales are at selling price. With a 25% margin, what is cost of goods sold, and then the stock that should have been there?
Excellent. If the goods were insured, the ₦18,000 becomes the basis of the insurance claim. Why must you use cost price, not selling price, for the claim?

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, adjusting expenses from cash records
examples.student_opening: A trader's cash book shows rent paid ₦48,000. Rent owing at start ₦4,000; rent owing at end ₦6,000. Rent expense?
examples.misconception: Student uses cash paid for rent as the rent expense without adjusting for accruals.

turns.text: A trader's cash book shows rent paid ₦48,000. Rent owing at start ₦4,000; rent owing at end ₦6,000. Rent expense?
Picture a shop owner who, in January, first cleared last year's ₦4,000 rent debt to the landlord, and in December still owes ₦6,000 for this year. Was all ₦48,000 for this year's use of the shop?
No — part was last year's rent, and some of this year's rent hasn't been paid.
So what's this year's true rent expense?
Right. In incomplete records, why is it so common for cash-book figures to need this kind of adjustment before they go into the profit and loss account?

examples.correct_understanding: Rent expense = paid ₦48,000 − opening accrual ₦4,000 + closing accrual ₦6,000 = ₦50,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, statement of affairs
examples.student_opening: Statement of affairs: shop fittings ₦90,000, stock ₦40,000, cash ₦10,000, creditors ₦15,000, loan from cooperative thrift society ₦50,000. I got capital ₦125,000.
examples.misconception: Student leaves out a long-term loan when computing capital in the statement of affairs.

turns.text: Statement of affairs: shop fittings ₦90,000, stock ₦40,000, cash ₦10,000, creditors ₦15,000, loan from cooperative thrift society ₦50,000. I got capital ₦125,000.
If the cooperative thrift society asked for its loan back today, whose money would the trader be returning — his own, or the society's?
The society's. So the loan isn't his capital.
Right — a loan is a liability even if it's repayable over years. Recompute capital including it.
Correct. In a proper balance sheet, would the loan go under current or non-current liabilities, and why?

examples.correct_understanding: Capital = assets ₦140,000 − creditors ₦15,000 − loan ₦50,000 = ₦75,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, statement of affairs
examples.student_opening: Delivery van ₦300,000, stock ₦50,000, debtors ₦25,000, creditors ₦30,000, bank overdraft ₦15,000. Is the overdraft an asset since it's the bank account?
examples.misconception: Student treats a bank overdraft as an asset (a bank balance) in the statement of affairs.

turns.text: Delivery van ₦300,000, stock ₦50,000, debtors ₦25,000, creditors ₦30,000, bank overdraft ₦15,000. Is the overdraft an asset since it's the bank account?
When your uncle 'goes into overdraft', is the bank holding his money for him, or has the bank lent him money he must pay back?
The bank has lent him money. He owes the bank.
So which side does the overdraft go on, and what's the capital?
Correct. If instead the bank statement had shown a positive balance of ₦15,000, how much would the capital change by?

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, statement of affairs
examples.student_opening: What's really the difference between a statement of affairs and a balance sheet? They both list assets and liabilities.
examples.misconception: Student thinks a statement of affairs is identical to a balance sheet in reliability and source of figures.

turns.text: What's really the difference between a statement of affairs and a balance sheet? They both list assets and liabilities.

Think of two ways to know a trader's worth. First: her full account books, where every transaction was recorded twice and balanced. Second: you visit her shop, count the stock, ask who owes her, and estimate the value of her old freezer. Which gives figures you can trust more, and why?
The full books — because the second way has estimates and could miss things.
So which of the two methods produces a balance sheet, and which produces a statement of affairs?
A balance sheet comes from double-entry records; a statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records, using estimates and physical counts, mainly to find capital.
Well put. Given those limitations, why do tax officers sometimes still insist on a statement of affairs for small traders?

examples.correct_understanding: A balance sheet is prepared from a complete double-entry system (figures drawn from ledger balances). A statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records, often using estimates and physical counts, mainly to determine capital (assets − liabilities).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, final accounts from incomplete records
examples.student_opening: I've reconstructed sales ₦104,000 and purchases ₦70,000 from a cooperative shop's cash records. Opening stock ₦10,000, closing stock ₦14,000. What now?
examples.misconception: Student does not see that reconstructed sales and purchases are then used in a normal trading account.

turns.text: I've reconstructed sales ₦104,000 and purchases ₦70,000 from a cooperative shop's cash records. Opening stock ₦10,000, closing stock ₦14,000. What now?
You've done the hard part — like a detective who has recovered the missing pieces of a torn receipt. Once the pieces are recovered, do you treat the receipt differently from any other receipt?
No, you just read it normally. So I just prepare a normal trading account.
Exactly. Find cost of goods sold and gross profit.
Correct. What would you need to reconstruct next to go from gross profit to net profit?

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, reconstructing income
examples.student_opening: An okada owner collects daily returns from his rider. In the year he received ₦520,000. At the start, the rider owed him ₦10,000 from last year; at the end, the rider owes ₦15,000. What's his income from returns for the year?
examples.misconception: Student takes cash received as income without adjusting for amounts owed at the start and end of the year.

turns.text: An okada owner collects daily returns from his rider. In the year he received ₦520,000. At the start, the rider owed him ₦10,000 from last year; at the end, the rider owes ₦15,000. What's his income from returns for the year?
When the rider paid off last year's ₦10,000 in January, was that for rides done this year?
No, last year. And the money he still owes at the end is for this year's rides.
So which amount do you remove from the cash received, and which do you add?
Correct. In the owner's statement of affairs at year end, how would you show the ₦15,000?

examples.correct_understanding: Income from returns = ₦520,000 − opening amount owed ₦10,000 + closing amount owed ₦15,000 = ₦525,000; the ₦15,000 is a debtor (current asset).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, statement of affairs
examples.student_opening: A tailor bought a sewing machine for ₦60,000 on 1 January; it should be depreciated by 10% per year. At 31 December she has fabric stock ₦20,000, cash ₦6,000, and owes a supplier ₦5,000. For capital, I used the machine at ₦60,000.
examples.misconception: Student includes a fixed asset at original cost in the closing statement of affairs instead of its depreciated value.

turns.text: A tailor bought a sewing machine for ₦60,000 on 1 January; it should be depreciated by 10% per year. At 31 December she has fabric stock ₦20,000, cash ₦6,000, and owes a supplier ₦5,000. For capital, I used the machine at ₦60,000.
If she tried to sell that machine after a full year of sewing Aso-ebi outfits, would a buyer pay the full brand-new price?
No, it's been used. It's worth less now.
So what value should the machine have in the statement of affairs, and what's her capital?
Correct. How would ignoring depreciation have affected her profit if you were comparing opening and closing capital?

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, profit versus cash
examples.student_opening: My uncle's building materials shop made ₦600,000 profit last year, but he says he has no money in the bank. How is that possible? Profit IS money.
examples.misconception: Student believes a business that made a profit must have that same amount of extra cash.

turns.text: My uncle's building materials shop made ₦600,000 profit last year, but he says he has no money in the bank. How is that possible? Profit IS money.
Think of a cement seller who gives contractors bags on credit — 'pay me when the client pays you'. When he records the sale, he has made a profit on paper. Has the cash entered his hand yet?
No, not until the contractor pays.
So profit is recorded when goods are sold, but cash comes when customers pay. Can you think of other things that could make profit and cash differ — for example, buying a new delivery truck?
Buying a truck takes a lot of cash, but only the depreciation hits profit. Also paying back a loan uses cash but isn't an expense.
Exactly. Which financial statement do accountants prepare specifically to explain why the cash balance changed, so your uncle can see where his ₦600,000 'went'?

examples.correct_understanding: Profit is measured on an accruals basis (sales when made, expenses when incurred), while cash moves when paid or received. Credit sales, stock build-up, capital purchases, loan repayments and drawings make cash differ from profit; the cash flow statement explains the change in cash.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, classification
examples.student_opening: A bakery bought a delivery van for ₦2,500,000 cash. In the cash flow statement, is that operating because the van is used to deliver bread?
examples.misconception: Student classifies the purchase of a delivery van as an operating cash outflow.

turns.text: A bakery bought a delivery van for ₦2,500,000 cash. In the cash flow statement, is that operating because the van is used to deliver bread?

Think of your family. Buying foodstuff every week is a regular running cost. Building a new room on the house is a big once-in-a-while outlay that serves for years. Which of these is more like buying the van?
Building the room — it's long-term.
Right. Cash flows are grouped into operating (day-to-day trading), investing (buying or selling long-term assets), and financing (money from or back to owners and lenders). So where does the van go?
Investing activities, as a cash outflow.
Correct. And the petrol the van uses every week to deliver bread — which section would that fall under?

examples.correct_understanding: Purchase of a delivery van is a cash outflow under investing activities because it is acquisition of a non-current asset; the van's running costs (fuel, etc.) are operating cash outflows.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, classification
examples.student_opening: Our business collected a ₦1,000,000 loan from the bank. Is that an operating inflow since it's money coming in?
examples.misconception: Student classifies a bank loan received as operating income.

turns.text: Our business collected a ₦1,000,000 loan from the bank. Is that an operating inflow since it's money coming in?
If a trader borrows ₦1m from a cooperative thrift society, has she EARNED that money by selling goods, or has she just raised funds that she must pay back?
She's raised funds. She didn't earn it.
So it doesn't belong with trading (operating) cash flows. Of investing and financing, which section deals with how the business is funded by owners and lenders?
Financing activities. So the loan is a financing inflow.
Exactly. When she later repays part of the loan, which section and which direction would that repayment appear in?

examples.correct_understanding: A loan received is a cash inflow from financing activities; repayments of the loan principal are financing outflows.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, classification
examples.student_opening: Payments to suppliers for stock — is that investing? The business is investing in goods.
examples.misconception: Student thinks payments to suppliers are investing activities because the business is 'investing in stock'.

turns.text: Payments to suppliers for stock — is that investing? The business is investing in goods.
A provisions seller at Mile 12 buys tomatoes every week and sells them within days. Is that like buying a shop building, or is it the everyday cycle of her business?
It's her everyday cycle.
So in the cash flow statement, is the section for the everyday trading cycle called operating, investing or financing?
Operating. So payments to suppliers are an operating cash outflow.
Correct. In everyday speech 'investing' can mean spending on anything useful, but in the cash flow statement it has a narrow meaning. What does it specifically refer to?

examples.correct_understanding: Payments to suppliers for trading stock are operating cash outflows; investing activities refer specifically to buying and selling long-term (non-current) assets and investments.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, non-cash items
examples.student_opening: Net profit ₦60,000, after charging depreciation of ₦15,000. Why does the cash flow statement ADD depreciation back? We already spent it!
examples.misconception: Student does not understand why depreciation is added back to profit in the operating section of the cash flow statement.

turns.text: Net profit ₦60,000, after charging depreciation of ₦15,000. Why does the cash flow statement ADD depreciation back? We already spent it!
Think of an okada owner who bought a bike three years ago. This year his accountant charged ₦15,000 depreciation on it. On what date did ₦15,000 actually leave his pocket for the bike THIS year?
I don't know. Didn't he pay for depreciation? I'm confused, just tell me the rule.

No problem. He paid for the bike in full three years ago — that cash left then. Depreciation this year is only a book entry spreading that old cost; NO cash leaves now. But it was subtracted when calculating the ₦60,000 profit. So to get from profit back to cash, what should you do with a deduction that involved no cash?
Hmm, undo it? But I'm still not sure what the final figure is.

Yes — undo it. Start from net profit ₦60,000. Depreciation of ₦15,000 reduced profit but not cash, so add it back: ₦60,000 + ₦15,000 = ₦75,000. That's the cash generated from operations before working capital changes. Adding back depreciation doesn't mean depreciation produces cash; it just cancels a non-cash deduction.

examples.correct_understanding: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it reduced profit but not cash, so it is added back: ₦60,000 + ₦15,000 = ₦75,000 before working capital changes.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, operating activities
examples.student_opening: Net profit ₦80,000; depreciation ₦10,000; debtors increased by ₦15,000; creditors increased by ₦5,000; stock decreased by ₦4,000. Net cash from operating activities? I added all: ₦114,000.
examples.misconception: Student adds every working capital change to profit regardless of whether it increased or decreased cash.

turns.text: Net profit ₦80,000; depreciation ₦10,000; debtors increased by ₦15,000; creditors increased by ₦5,000; stock decreased by ₦4,000. Net cash from operating activities? I added all: ₦114,000.
Think of a POS agent. If more of her customers now owe her money than last year — debtors up by ₦15,000 — does she have more cash in hand, or less?
Less, I think? But then creditors and stock... I'm totally confused. Abeg show me.

You're right about debtors — more customers owing means less cash, so SUBTRACT the increase. Now the rule for the other two: creditors increasing means she hasn't paid suppliers yet — cash stays with her, so ADD. Stock decreasing means she sold off stock without replacing it — cash freed up, so ADD. Try ₦80,000 + ₦10,000 − ₦15,000 + ₦5,000 + ₦4,000.
I want to be sure I'm doing it in the right order. Can you walk me through it?

Sure:
Net profit ₦80,000
Add depreciation ₦10,000 → ₦90,000
Less increase in debtors ₦15,000 → ₦75,000
Add increase in creditors ₦5,000 → ₦80,000
Add decrease in stock ₦4,000 → ₦84,000
Net cash from operating activities = ₦84,000. Rule: increase in a current asset → subtract; increase in a current liability → add (and the reverse for decreases).

examples.correct_understanding: Operating cash flow = ₦80,000 + depreciation ₦10,000 − increase in debtors ₦15,000 + increase in creditors ₦5,000 + decrease in stock ₦4,000 = ₦84,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, working capital
examples.student_opening: Profit is ₦50,000. Stock went UP by ₦12,000 this year. More stock is good, so I added it to get ₦62,000 operating cash flow.
examples.misconception: Student adds an increase in stock to profit in the operating section, thinking more stock means more cash.

turns.text: Profit is ₦50,000. Stock went UP by ₦12,000 this year. More stock is good, so I added it to get ₦62,000 operating cash flow.
An Alaba trader filled his shop with extra TVs this year — ₦12,000 worth more than last year. Where did the money to buy those extra TVs come from?
From his cash. So the cash was used to buy stock that is just sitting there.
So does an increase in stock increase or reduce cash? Recalculate.
Correct. Having more stock may be good for business, but it ties up cash. What would the adjustment have been if stock had fallen by the same amount?

examples.correct_understanding: An increase in stock uses cash, so it is deducted: ₦50,000 − ₦12,000 = ₦38,000 (ignoring other adjustments).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, working capital
examples.student_opening: Profit ₦45,000; creditors increased by ₦8,000. Creditors are debts, so debts reduce cash — I subtracted to get ₦37,000.
examples.misconception: Student subtracts an increase in creditors, treating it as a cost that reduces cash.

turns.text: Profit ₦45,000; creditors increased by ₦8,000. Creditors are debts, so debts reduce cash — I subtracted to get ₦37,000.
Suppose a mama-put collected foodstuff worth ₦8,000 more from her market woman on credit this year than last year. While she hasn't paid, where is that ₦8,000?
Still in her own purse.
So does an increase in creditors leave the business with more cash or less than profit suggests? Recalculate.
Correct. Why is relying on this forever a risky way to 'find cash'?

examples.correct_understanding: An increase in creditors means cash has not yet been paid out, so it is added: ₦45,000 + ₦8,000 = ₦53,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, net change in cash
examples.student_opening: Net cash from operating ₦84,000, net cash used in investing ₦120,000, net cash from financing ₦50,000. Cash at start ₦20,000. Find closing cash. I got ₦254,000 and it's way too much.
examples.misconception: Student adds all three section totals as positive numbers, ignoring that investing was a net outflow, and forgets the opening cash balance.

turns.text: Net cash from operating ₦84,000, net cash used in investing ₦120,000, net cash from financing ₦50,000. Cash at start ₦20,000. Find closing cash. I got ₦254,000 and it's way too much.

Think of a cooperative's three money streams: the members' trading brought money in, buying a grinding machine took money out, and a loan brought money in. When you add them, should every stream have the same sign?
I don't know. The question says 'net cash used in investing' — I just added it. Please just do it.

The word 'used' is the key — it means cash went OUT. So investing is −₦120,000, not +. Now combine: ₦84,000 − ₦120,000 + ₦50,000 gives the net change for the year. Then remember the business didn't start with zero. What's the net change?
₦14,000? But how does that become the closing figure?

Right, net increase in cash = ₦84,000 − ₦120,000 + ₦50,000 = ₦14,000.
Add cash at beginning of year ₦20,000.
Cash at end of year = ₦20,000 + ₦14,000 = ₦34,000.
This closing figure should agree with the cash/bank balance in the balance sheet — that's the check that the statement is right.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, classification
examples.student_opening: Where do drawings go in a sole trader's cash flow statement? I put them in operating as an expense.
examples.misconception: Student classifies drawings as an operating expense in the cash flow statement.

turns.text: Where do drawings go in a sole trader's cash flow statement? I put them in operating as an expense.
When a Kano grain merchant takes ₦100,000 from the business for his daughter's wedding, is that a cost of running the business or money going back to the owner?
Money going back to the owner.
Which cash flow section deals with the business's relationship with its owners and lenders?
Financing. So drawings are a financing outflow.
Correct. For a limited company, what's the equivalent of drawings, and where would it appear?

examples.correct_understanding: Drawings are a cash outflow under financing activities because they are payments to the owner, not operating expenses (for companies, dividends paid are the equivalent).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, disposal of assets
examples.student_opening: A firm sold equipment with book value ₦35,000 for ₦40,000. Profit includes a ₦5,000 gain. In the cash flow statement I left the gain in profit AND put ₦40,000 in investing. Is that fine?
examples.misconception: Student includes the gain on disposal in operating cash inflow and also counts the full proceeds, double counting.

turns.text: A firm sold equipment with book value ₦35,000 for ₦40,000. Profit includes a ₦5,000 gain. In the cash flow statement I left the gain in profit AND put ₦40,000 in investing. Is that fine?
A trader sells his old freezer for ₦40,000. How much cash actually came in from that sale — ₦40,000, or ₦40,000 plus ₦5,000?
But your statement shows ₦40,000 in investing AND the ₦5,000 gain hidden inside profit in operating. What must you do to the gain in the operating section so the sale is only counted once?
Subtract the ₦5,000 gain from profit in the operating section, and keep the full ₦40,000 in investing.
Exactly. Following the same logic, what would you do with a LOSS on disposal in the operating section?

examples.correct_understanding: Proceeds of ₦40,000 are an investing inflow; the ₦5,000 gain is deducted from profit in the operating section to avoid double counting (a loss on disposal would be added back).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, liquidity
examples.student_opening: A POS agent's business is growing fast and making good profit, but she keeps running out of float to pay customers. How can profit be high and cash be low?
examples.misconception: Student believes a growing, profitable business cannot run into cash problems.

turns.text: A POS agent's business is growing fast and making good profit, but she keeps running out of float to pay customers. How can profit be high and cash be low?
Suppose she started giving cash-out to trusted market women on credit, 'pay me back at close of market', and she opened two more kiosks this month. Where is her cash sitting now?
With the market women who owe her, and in the new kiosks.
So the profit is real, but cash is tied up in debtors and new assets. In the cash flow statement, which sections would show those two drains?
Increase in debtors reduces operating cash flow, and the new kiosks are investing outflows.
Correct. Accountants call expanding faster than your cash can support 'overtrading'. What are two things she could do to protect her float?

examples.correct_understanding: A profitable business can run short of cash when growth ties cash up in debtors, stock and new assets (overtrading); the cash flow statement reveals this through working capital changes in operating activities and outflows in investing activities.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, purpose
examples.student_opening: Why do we need a cash flow statement if the income statement already shows profit?
examples.misconception: Student thinks the cash flow statement repeats information already in the income statement.

turns.text: Why do we need a cash flow statement if the income statement already shows profit?

Imagine the treasurer of an Aso-ebi committee reporting to the bride. One report says 'we made ₦200,000 profit on fabric'. Another says 'this is exactly where every naira came from and where it went, and why only ₦30,000 is in the account'. Which report would help the bride know if she can pay the caterer tomorrow?
The second one — it's about actual cash.
So what question does the income statement answer, and what question does the cash flow statement answer?
Income statement: did we make a profit? Cash flow statement: where did cash come from and go, and why did the cash balance change?
Well put. Who, apart from the owner, would particularly care about the cash flow statement — think of someone about to lend the business money?
