examples.correct_understanding: The income statement measures profit on an accruals basis; the cash flow statement shows sources and uses of cash under operating, investing and financing activities, explaining the change in cash and helping assess liquidity.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, non-cash items
examples.student_opening: A transport business made a net loss of ₦10,000, but depreciation on its buses was ₦30,000. No working capital changes. Its operating cash flow must be negative, right?
examples.misconception: Student assumes a net loss must mean negative operating cash flow.

turns.text: A transport business made a net loss of ₦10,000, but depreciation on its buses was ₦30,000. No working capital changes. Its operating cash flow must be negative, right?

The buses were paid for years ago. This year, the ₦30,000 depreciation was deducted in the accounts but no cash left the business for it. Would the business's cash be worse or better than the loss suggests?
Better — the depreciation made the loss look worse without taking cash.
So start from the loss and add back the depreciation. What do you get?
−₦10,000 + ₦30,000 = ₦20,000, a positive operating cash flow.
Correct. Why might this business still be in trouble in the long run even though its cash flow is positive now?

examples.correct_understanding: Operating cash flow = net loss (−₦10,000) + depreciation ₦30,000 = ₦20,000 inflow; a loss-making business can still have positive operating cash flow because of non-cash expenses.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, financing activities
examples.student_opening: Capital introduced ₦100,000, loan repaid ₦40,000, drawings ₦25,000. Net cash from financing — is it ₦165,000?
examples.misconception: Student adds loan repayments and drawings to capital introduced instead of deducting them.

turns.text: Capital introduced ₦100,000, loan repaid ₦40,000, drawings ₦25,000. Net cash from financing — is it ₦165,000?
Think of the owner's pocket and the lender's pocket as two taps into the business's tank. Capital introduced flows IN. What direction do loan repayment and drawings flow?
Out — money goes back to the lender and the owner.
So which items get a minus sign, and what's the net figure?
Correct — a net inflow from financing. If drawings had been ₦90,000 instead, what would the net financing figure be, and how would you describe it?

examples.correct_understanding: Net cash from financing = ₦100,000 − ₦40,000 − ₦25,000 = ₦35,000 inflow.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, cash flow statement, investing activities
examples.student_opening: A block-making business bought a new machine for ₦150,000 and sold its old van for ₦40,000. Net cash used in investing?
examples.misconception: Student omits the proceeds from selling an old asset when computing net investing cash flow.

turns.text: A block-making business bought a new machine for ₦150,000 and sold its old van for ₦40,000. Net cash used in investing?
When a farmer buys a new tractor and at the same time sells his old one, how much of his own cash did the swap actually use up?
The cost of the new one minus what he got for the old one.
Apply that here.
₦150,000 − ₦40,000 = ₦110,000 net cash used in investing.
Correct. In the statement, should you show the two items separately or just the net figure? Why might examiners prefer one over the other?

examples.correct_understanding: Net cash used in investing = purchase ₦150,000 − proceeds ₦40,000 = ₦110,000 outflow (items are usually shown separately, then netted).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, purpose of control accounts
examples.student_opening: Why do we need a sales ledger control account when every customer already has their own account in the sales ledger? It's just double work.
examples.misconception: Student thinks control accounts are just an extra, pointless copy of the personal ledgers.

turns.text: Why do we need a sales ledger control account when every customer already has their own account in the sales ledger? It's just double work.

Picture an Alaba market wholesaler with 300 retailers buying on credit, each with a page in his big book. His boss asks 'how much do ALL our customers owe us right now?' and also 'can you prove no page has an error?' Would flipping through 300 pages be the fastest way?
No — it would take forever, and he could still miss an error.

Now suppose there's ONE summary account that is posted with TOTALS — total credit sales, total cash received, and so on. If its balance agrees with the sum of the 300 individual balances, what does that tell the boss?
That the individual ledgers are probably correct, and he gets the total owed quickly.
Exactly. If the totals DIDN'T agree, how would control accounts help him narrow down where to look for the error?

examples.correct_understanding: A sales ledger control account summarises (in totals) all transactions with credit customers. It gives the total debtors figure quickly, checks the arithmetical accuracy of the sales ledger, helps locate errors to a particular ledger, and deters fraud.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, sales ledger control account entries
examples.student_opening: Credit sales go on the credit side of the sales ledger control account, since they're 'credit' sales. Correct?
examples.misconception: Student places total credit sales on the credit side of the sales ledger control account.

turns.text: Credit sales go on the credit side of the sales ledger control account, since they're 'credit' sales. Correct?
When a tailor sews a dress for a customer on credit, does the customer now owe the tailor MORE or LESS than before?
More.
The sales ledger control account is really a summary of what customers owe — an asset. On which side does an asset increase?
The debit side. So credit sales are debited in the sales ledger control account. The 'credit' just means sold on credit terms.
Correct — the word 'credit' in 'credit sales' is about payment terms, not the ledger side. Name two items that go on the CREDIT side of this account.

examples.correct_understanding: Credit sales increase amounts owed by customers (an asset), so they are debited in the sales ledger control account; 'credit' refers to payment terms. Cash received, discounts allowed, returns inwards and bad debts are credited.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, sales ledger control account
examples.student_opening: Prepare the sales ledger control account for January: balance b/d ₦45,000, credit sales ₦210,000, cash received from debtors ₦180,000, discount allowed ₦4,000, returns inwards ₦6,000, bad debts written off ₦3,000. Find the balance c/d. I have no idea where to put half of these.
examples.misconception: Student cannot decide which items reduce the debtors total and places some on the wrong side.

turns.text: Prepare the sales ledger control account for January: balance b/d ₦45,000, credit sales ₦210,000, cash received from debtors ₦180,000, discount allowed ₦4,000, returns inwards ₦6,000, bad debts written off ₦3,000. Find the balance c/d. I have no idea where to put half of these.
Think of the Alaba wholesaler's 'who owes me' book. Go item by item: when a retailer RETURNS a faulty TV, does that retailer owe more or less?
Less, I guess. But discount and bad debts — I don't know. Just show me please.

Good — returns reduce what's owed. The same is true for discount allowed (you forgave part of the debt) and bad debts (you gave up on it). So: items that INCREASE debts — opening balance and credit sales — go on the debit side. Everything that REDUCES debts — cash, discount, returns, bad debts — goes on the credit side. Total the debit side first.
Debit side is ₦255,000. I still don't know how to get the balance.

Here's the full account:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d | 45,000 |  |
| 31 Jan | Credit sales | 210,000 |  |
| 31 Jan | Cash received |  | 180,000 |
| 31 Jan | Discount allowed |  | 4,000 |
| 31 Jan | Returns inwards |  | 6,000 |
| 31 Jan | Bad debts |  | 3,000 |
| 31 Jan | Balance c/d |  | 62,000 |
|  | Total | 255,000 | 255,000 |
Working: ₦255,000 − (₦180,000 + ₦4,000 + ₦6,000 + ₦3,000 = ₦193,000) = ₦62,000. This ₦62,000 balance c/d should equal the total of all individual debtors' balances in the sales ledger.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, purchases ledger control account
examples.student_opening: Purchases ledger control account: balance b/d ₦30,000, credit purchases ₦150,000, paid to creditors ₦130,000, discount received ₦3,000, returns outwards ₦5,000. I put the opening balance on the debit side like debtors.
examples.misconception: Student sets up the purchases ledger control account like the sales ledger control account, with the opening balance on the debit side.

turns.text: Purchases ledger control account: balance b/d ₦30,000, credit purchases ₦150,000, paid to creditors ₦130,000, discount received ₦3,000, returns outwards ₦5,000. I put the opening balance on the debit side like debtors.
Is the purchases ledger control account about people who owe US, or people WE owe — like the distributor who supplies a provisions shop on credit?
People we owe. So it's a liability.
And on which side does a liability's balance sit? So where do the opening balance and credit purchases go, and where do payments, discount received and returns outwards go?
Credit side: opening balance and purchases. Debit side: payments, discount received, returns outwards. Balance = ₦180,000 − ₦138,000 = ₦42,000.

Correct. Here it is laid out:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d |  | 30,000 |
| 31 Jan | Credit purchases |  | 150,000 |
| 31 Jan | Bank (paid to creditors) | 130,000 |  |
| 31 Jan | Discount received | 3,000 |  |
| 31 Jan | Returns outwards | 5,000 |  |
| 31 Jan | Balance c/d | 42,000 |  |
|  | Total | 180,000 | 180,000 |
It's the mirror image of the sales ledger control account. Where does the ₦42,000 appear in the balance sheet?

examples.correct_understanding: The purchases ledger control account is a liability account: closing balance = ₦30,000 + ₦150,000 − ₦130,000 − ₦3,000 − ₦5,000 = ₦42,000 (credit balance), shown as trade creditors under current liabilities.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, items excluded from control accounts
examples.student_opening: Should I include cash sales of ₦80,000 in the sales ledger control account along with credit sales?
examples.misconception: Student includes cash sales in the sales ledger control account.

turns.text: Should I include cash sales of ₦80,000 in the sales ledger control account along with credit sales?
When someone buys bread from a kiosk and pays cash on the spot, does the kiosk owner write that person's name in her 'owing' notebook?
No — they've paid already, nobody owes.
And the sales ledger control account is a summary of that 'owing' notebook. So does the ₦80,000 belong there?
No. Cash sales never create a debtor, so they're left out of the control account.
Correct. Can you think of another item examiners like to slip into control account questions that should also be left out?

examples.correct_understanding: Cash sales do not create debtors and are excluded from the sales ledger control account; only transactions affecting credit customers are included.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, contra entries between control accounts
examples.student_opening: Mr Okafor buys from us on credit AND supplies us on credit. We agreed to set off ₦7,500 he owes us against what we owe him. How do I record that in the control accounts?
examples.misconception: Student does not know how to record a set-off where the same person is both a debtor and a creditor.

turns.text: Mr Okafor buys from us on credit AND supplies us on credit. We agreed to set off ₦7,500 he owes us against what we owe him. How do I record that in the control accounts?

You owe your friend ₦7,500 for recharge cards, and he owes you ₦7,500 for a phone charger. Instead of exchanging cash back and forth, you both say 'we're square'. After that, what happens to what you owe him AND what he owes you?
Both go down... but I don't know which control account gets debited. Just tell me.

Okay, let's use the sides you know. What he owes us is in the sales ledger control account (an asset) — to reduce an asset you... credit it. What we owe him is in the purchases ledger control account (a liability) — to reduce a liability you... debit it. So which account is debited?
The purchases ledger control? I'm not fully sure.

Yes, that's right. The journal is:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 30 Jun | Purchases ledger control | 7,500 |  |
| 30 Jun | Sales ledger control |  | 7,500 |
Debit purchases ledger control (our debt to him falls by ₦7,500); credit sales ledger control (his debt to us falls by ₦7,500). Both balances drop by the same amount — exactly like you and your friend 'cancelling' your debts.

examples.correct_understanding: A contra (set-off) is recorded by debiting the purchases ledger control account and crediting the sales ledger control account with ₦7,500.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, dishonoured cheques in control accounts
examples.student_opening: A customer's cheque for ₦12,000 bounced. The cheque had been credited in the sales ledger control account when received. What now — do I credit it again?
examples.misconception: Student credits the sales ledger control account for a dishonoured cheque, treating it as another receipt.

turns.text: A customer's cheque for ₦12,000 bounced. The cheque had been credited in the sales ledger control account when received. What now — do I credit it again?
A customer pays you with a transfer that later gets reversed by the bank. Before the reversal you cleaned her name out of your owing book. After the reversal, does she still owe you?
Yes, she still owes me. The payment didn't really happen.
So the debt comes back. To restore an asset in the sales ledger control account, which side do you post it to?
Debit side — debit sales ledger control ₦12,000, credit bank.
Correct. What should the business also do in the customer's individual account in the sales ledger?

examples.correct_understanding: A dishonoured cheque reinstates the debt: debit the sales ledger control account (and the customer's personal account) with ₦12,000, credit bank.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, credit balances in sales ledger
examples.student_opening: The question says the sales ledger control account has a debit balance of ₦90,000 AND a credit balance of ₦2,000 at the start. How can a debtors account have a credit balance?
examples.misconception: Student thinks a sales ledger control account cannot have a credit balance and nets it off silently.

turns.text: The question says the sales ledger control account has a debit balance of ₦90,000 AND a credit balance of ₦2,000 at the start. How can a debtors account have a credit balance?
Suppose a customer at your mum's provisions shop paid ₦2,000 extra by mistake, or returned goods after already paying. Who now owes whom?
The shop owes the customer ₦2,000.
So within the sales ledger, most customers owe the business, but a few are owed BY the business. How would that ₦2,000 appear in the control account, and where in the balance sheet?
As a credit balance in the control account, and in the balance sheet it's a current liability, not netted against debtors.
Correct. Why do accountants avoid simply netting the ₦2,000 against the ₦90,000?

examples.correct_understanding: A credit balance in the sales ledger arises when customers have overpaid or returned goods after payment; it is shown as a credit balance b/d in the sales ledger control account and as a current liability, not netted against debtors.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, limitations of control accounts
examples.student_opening: My control account agrees with the total of the sales ledger balances. So the sales ledger is 100% error-free?
examples.misconception: Student believes agreement of the control account with the ledger totals proves there are no errors.

turns.text: My control account agrees with the total of the sales ledger balances. So the sales ledger is 100% error-free?
Two market women each owe a trader ₦5,000. The trader records Mama Nkechi's ₦5,000 payment in Mama Ngozi's account by mistake. Does the total of all the customers' balances change?
No — the total is the same, just the wrong person's account was reduced.
So would the control account catch that error? What kinds of errors do you think a control account CANNOT detect?
It can't catch posting to the wrong customer's account, or an invoice left out completely from both, or compensating errors.
Exactly. So what does agreement really prove, and what does it not prove?

examples.correct_understanding: Agreement of a control account with the ledger total proves arithmetical accuracy only; it does not detect errors of commission (wrong personal account), complete omission, original entry or compensating errors.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, purchases ledger control account
examples.student_opening:
Check my purchases ledger control account:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Mar | Balance b/d |  | 20,000 |
| 31 Mar | Credit purchases |  | 60,000 |
| 31 Mar | Discount received |  | 2,000 |
| 31 Mar | Bank | 50,000 |  |
| 31 Mar | Balance c/d | 32,000 |  |
|  | Total | 82,000 | 82,000 |
The total list of creditors from the ledger is ₦28,000, not ₦32,000. Where's my mistake?
examples.misconception: Student posts discount received to the credit side of the purchases ledger control account, increasing instead of reducing the creditors balance.

turns.text:
Check my purchases ledger control account:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Mar | Balance b/d |  | 20,000 |
| 31 Mar | Credit purchases |  | 60,000 |
| 31 Mar | Discount received |  | 2,000 |
| 31 Mar | Bank | 50,000 |  |
| 31 Mar | Balance c/d | 32,000 |  |
|  | Total | 82,000 | 82,000 |
The total list of creditors from the ledger is ₦28,000, not ₦32,000. Where's my mistake?
When a Kano supplier tells you 'because you paid early, forget the last ₦2,000', do you now owe him more or less?
Less.
In this account, credits increase what you owe. Where did you put the discount received, and where should it go?
I put it on the credit side. It should be on the debit side because it reduces what we owe. Then the balance is ₦80,000 − ₦50,000 − ₦2,000 = ₦28,000.
Now it agrees with the ledger. Notice the difference was ₦4,000 — twice the discount. Why is 'difference = twice an amount' a useful clue when hunting errors?

examples.correct_understanding: Discount received reduces creditors and belongs on the debit side of the purchases ledger control account; the corrected balance is ₦20,000 + ₦60,000 − ₦50,000 − ₦2,000 = ₦28,000.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, items excluded from control accounts
examples.student_opening: The question gives bad debts ₦4,000 and an increase in provision for doubtful debts ₦3,000. I credited both to the sales ledger control account.
examples.misconception: Student includes the provision for doubtful debts in the sales ledger control account as if it were a bad debt.

turns.text: The question gives bad debts ₦4,000 and an increase in provision for doubtful debts ₦3,000. I credited both to the sales ledger control account.

A trader writes off a customer who has run away to Ghana — that name is struck out of the owing book. Another customer is just paying slowly, so the trader 'sets aside' some money in his mind in case she doesn't pay. Is the slow payer's name struck out of the owing book?
No, she still owes. He's just being careful.
So which of the two actually changes the individual customers' balances in the sales ledger — and so belongs in the control account?
Only the bad debts. The provision is kept in its own account and deducted from debtors in the balance sheet.
Correct. Which accounting concept is behind creating the provision in the first place?

examples.correct_understanding: Bad debts written off are credited to the sales ledger control account because individual debtor balances are reduced; the provision for doubtful debts is kept in a separate provision account (not in the control account) and deducted from debtors in the balance sheet, reflecting prudence.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, sales ledger control account entries
examples.student_opening: Our business charged interest of ₦1,500 on overdue customer accounts. Where does that go in the sales ledger control account?
examples.misconception: Student does not know how to record interest charged to customers on overdue accounts.

turns.text: Our business charged interest of ₦1,500 on overdue customer accounts. Where does that go in the sales ledger control account?
Think of an Esusu collector who adds a small charge when someone's contribution is late. After adding the charge, does the member owe more or less?
More.
So in the sales ledger control account, which side records things that make customers owe more?
The debit side. So debit sales ledger control ₦1,500 and credit interest received.
Correct. Where would the interest received appear in the final accounts?

examples.correct_understanding: Interest charged on overdue accounts increases amounts owed: debit the sales ledger control account (and customers' accounts), credit interest receivable, which is income in the profit and loss account.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, consignment, consignor and consignee
examples.student_opening: An Aba shoemaker sends 200 pairs of shoes to an agent in Lagos to sell on his behalf for a commission. Who is the consignor and who is the consignee? And do the shoes now belong to the Lagos agent?
examples.misconception: Student confuses the consignor and consignee and thinks ownership passes when goods are sent.

turns.text: An Aba shoemaker sends 200 pairs of shoes to an agent in Lagos to sell on his behalf for a commission. Who is the consignor and who is the consignee? And do the shoes now belong to the Lagos agent?
Think of a farmer in Benue who sends yams to a trader in Lagos: 'sell them for me, keep 5% for your trouble, send me the rest'. Until a buyer pays, whose yams are they?
Still the farmer's. The trader is just selling for him.
So in your shoe example, who is the owner who sends the goods, and who is the agent who receives and sells them? Match them to 'consignor' and 'consignee'.
The Aba shoemaker is the consignor — he sends. The Lagos agent is the consignee — he receives and sells. Ownership stays with the shoemaker until the shoes are sold.
Correct. Because ownership doesn't pass, should the shoemaker record the dispatch of shoes as a sale?

examples.correct_understanding: The consignor (Aba shoemaker) sends goods to the consignee (Lagos agent) who sells them on the consignor's behalf for a commission; ownership remains with the consignor until the goods are sold to third parties.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, consignment, pro-forma invoice
examples.student_opening: The consignor sent goods to the agent with a pro-forma invoice for ₦300,000. Why can't I record ₦300,000 as sales? There's an invoice!
examples.misconception: Student treats goods sent on consignment (with a pro-forma invoice) as sales to the consignee.

turns.text: The consignor sent goods to the agent with a pro-forma invoice for ₦300,000. Why can't I record ₦300,000 as sales? There's an invoice!
When your aunt sends a bag of garri to a relative in Abuja to sell for her, with a note 'sell at about ₦300,000 total', has the relative BOUGHT the garri from her?
No, he's just holding it to sell. The note is only a guide.
A pro-forma invoice plays the role of that note. So what should the consignor debit when the goods are sent, and what should be credited instead of sales?
Debit consignment account (to the agent) and credit 'goods sent on consignment' — at cost — not sales.
Correct. When will the consignor finally recognise a sale, and on what document will he rely to know the amount?

examples.correct_understanding: Goods sent on consignment are not sales: the consignor debits a consignment account and credits goods sent on consignment (at cost). A pro-forma invoice is only for information; sales are recognised when the consignee reports them in an account sales.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, consignment account and profit
examples.student_opening: Goods costing ₦200,000 sent on consignment; consignor paid freight ₦20,000. Consignee sold all for ₦350,000, paid selling expenses ₦8,000, and is entitled to 5% commission on sales. Find profit on consignment. I got ₦130,000.
examples.misconception: Student omits the consignee's commission and expenses when computing profit on consignment.

turns.text: Goods costing ₦200,000 sent on consignment; consignor paid freight ₦20,000. Consignee sold all for ₦350,000, paid selling expenses ₦8,000, and is entitled to 5% commission on sales. Find profit on consignment. I got ₦130,000.
Think of the Benue yam farmer again. When the Lagos trader sends money back, does he send the FULL sales amount, or does he first keep something?
He keeps his commission I think. But I don't know what else. Please show me, I'm tired of guessing.

You got the commission right. He ALSO takes out any expenses he paid on the farmer's behalf. So the consignor bears four costs: goods ₦200,000, his own freight ₦20,000, the consignee's expenses ₦8,000, and commission at 5% of sales. What is 5% of ₦350,000?
₦17,500. But I'm still not sure how it all comes together.

Here's the consignment account in the consignor's books:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Feb | Goods sent on consignment | 200,000 |  |
| 1 Feb | Cash (freight paid by consignor) | 20,000 |  |
| 30 Apr | Consignee: expenses | 8,000 |  |
| 30 Apr | Consignee: commission | 17,500 |  |
| 30 Apr | Consignee: sales |  | 350,000 |
| 30 Apr | Profit on consignment | 104,500 |  |
|  | Total | 350,000 | 350,000 |
Profit = ₦350,000 − (₦200,000 + ₦20,000 + ₦8,000 + ₦17,500) = ₦104,500. Your ₦130,000 left out the consignee's expenses and commission.

examples.correct_understanding: Profit on consignment = sales ₦350,000 − goods ₦200,000 − freight ₦20,000 − consignee's expenses ₦8,000 − commission 5% (₦17,500) = ₦104,500.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, consignment, valuation of unsold stock
examples.student_opening: 100 bags of rice costing ₦1,000 each were sent on consignment; the consignor paid freight of ₦10,000 to get them to the consignee. 20 bags are unsold at year end. I valued them at ₦20,000.
examples.misconception: Student values unsold consignment stock at bare purchase cost, ignoring the proportion of the consignor's freight.

turns.text: 100 bags of rice costing ₦1,000 each were sent on consignment; the consignor paid freight of ₦10,000 to get them to the consignee. 20 bags are unsold at year end. I valued them at ₦20,000.
A bag of rice sitting in the Lagos agent's store has cost the owner its price in Kano PLUS its share of the lorry to Lagos. Would the owner be happy to value it as if it were still in Kano?
No — it cost more to bring it to Lagos.
So what is the full cost per bag including its share of freight, and what are the unsold bags worth?
Correct. Why would the consignee's SELLING expenses (like advertising) NOT be added to the value of unsold stock?

examples.correct_understanding: Unsold stock is valued at cost plus a proportionate share of the consignor's freight: (₦100,000 + ₦10,000) ÷ 100 = ₦1,100 per bag × 20 = ₦22,000; selling expenses are excluded.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, joint venture, meaning
examples.student_opening: Ade and Bola bought one container of Aso-ebi lace together to sell for a big wedding, then they'll go their separate ways. Is that a partnership?
examples.misconception: Student confuses a joint venture with a partnership.

turns.text: Ade and Bola bought one container of Aso-ebi lace together to sell for a big wedding, then they'll go their separate ways. Is that a partnership?

Think of two neighbours who contribute money to buy one cow for Sallah, share the meat, and that's the end of it. Compare that with two sisters who open a shop together to run for years. Which is Ade and Bola's arrangement more like?
The cow for Sallah — it's just for one deal.
Right. Accountants call a temporary association for a specific venture a 'joint venture'. What's the key difference from a partnership, and what happens when the lace is sold out?
A partnership is continuing; a joint venture is for a specific, short-term project and ends when the project is done. They share the profit and end it.
Correct. If they don't agree a profit-sharing ratio, how do you think the profit would normally be shared?

examples.correct_understanding: A joint venture is a temporary association of two or more persons for a specific business undertaking, which ends when the venture is completed; unlike a partnership, it is not a continuing business. Profit is shared in the agreed ratio (equally if no agreement).

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, memorandum joint venture account
examples.student_opening: Joint venture: Ade paid ₦300,000 for the lace; Bola paid ₦40,000 for transport and storage. They sold all of it for ₦500,000. Profit shared equally. I said each gets ₦250,000.
examples.misconception: Student shares the joint venture sales rather than the profit, or forgets costs paid by the other venturer.

turns.text: Joint venture: Ade paid ₦300,000 for the lace; Bola paid ₦40,000 for transport and storage. They sold all of it for ₦500,000. Profit shared equally. I said each gets ₦250,000.

Back to the two neighbours and the Sallah cow. If one paid for the cow and the other paid for the butcher, and they sold some meat, would they share the SALE money straight down the middle, or first give each person back what they spent?
I don't know how to handle two people's costs. Please just show me.
Okay. First find the venture's total profit, ignoring who paid what: sales ₦500,000 minus ALL costs (Ade's ₦300,000 and Bola's ₦40,000). Then share that profit equally. What's the total profit?
₦160,000? And then half each? I'm not sure how to show it.

Exactly right. Here's the memorandum joint venture account:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 May | Purchases (paid by Ade) | 300,000 |  |
| 1 May | Expenses (paid by Bola) | 40,000 |  |
| 30 Jun | Sales |  | 500,000 |
| 30 Jun | Share of profit: Ade | 80,000 |  |
| 30 Jun | Share of profit: Bola | 80,000 |  |
|  | Total | 500,000 | 500,000 |
Profit = ₦500,000 − ₦300,000 − ₦40,000 = ₦160,000, so each gets ₦80,000. Then, in settlement, Ade is entitled to ₦300,000 + ₦80,000 = ₦380,000 and Bola to ₦40,000 + ₦80,000 = ₦120,000, which together equal the ₦500,000 sales.

examples.correct_understanding: Joint venture profit = ₦500,000 − ₦300,000 − ₦40,000 = ₦160,000, shared equally (₦80,000 each); Ade receives ₦380,000 and Bola ₦120,000 in total.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, joint venture records
examples.student_opening: In a joint venture where no separate books are kept, does each venturer record ALL the transactions of the venture in their own books?
examples.misconception: Student thinks each venturer records the whole joint venture in their own books.

turns.text: In a joint venture where no separate books are kept, does each venturer record ALL the transactions of the venture in their own books?
When two friends contribute for a wedding gift, does each one write in their personal notebook what the OTHER person spent, or only what they themselves spent and what the other person owes them?
Only what they spent themselves, and the balance with the other friend.
So each venturer keeps a 'joint venture with [other party]' account for their own transactions. Where, then, would you bring ALL the transactions together to find the total profit?
In a memorandum joint venture account — it's not part of either person's double entry, just a statement to calculate the profit.
Correct. After the profit is known, what does each venturer do in their own 'joint venture with' account before settling up?

examples.correct_understanding: Where separate books are not kept, each venturer records only their own transactions in a 'joint venture with [co-venturer]' account; a memorandum joint venture account (outside the double entry) combines all transactions to compute total profit, and each party then credits their share of profit before settlement.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, public sector accounting, consolidated revenue fund
examples.student_opening: If the immigration service collects passport fees, can it just spend that money on its own needs?
examples.misconception: Student thinks each government ministry keeps and spends its own revenue freely.

turns.text: If the immigration service collects passport fees, can it just spend that money on its own needs?

In many families, the children who work give their earnings to a common family purse, and spending comes out of that purse only after the family agrees. Why might a family insist on one central purse instead of each child spending what they collect?
So there's control, and money is shared according to the family's priorities.
Government uses the same idea. What do you think the central 'purse' into which government revenues are paid is called?
The Consolidated Revenue Fund? So passport fees go there, not straight to immigration.
That's the idea. And to spend from that fund, what approval do you think is needed — can the President or Governor just withdraw at will?

examples.correct_understanding: Government revenues are generally paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the main government account), and withdrawals from it require legislative authorisation (e.g. an Appropriation Act), ensuring control over public funds.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, public sector accounting, sources of revenue
examples.student_opening: Isn't oil the ONLY way the Nigerian government gets money?
examples.misconception: Student thinks the government's only source of revenue is oil.

turns.text: Isn't oil the ONLY way the Nigerian government gets money?

Think of what your family pays to government in a year — when your dad pays tax from his salary, when your mum pays a market levy, or when someone pays a fine for breaking a traffic rule. Who receives those payments?
Government. So there are taxes, levies and fines too.
Right. Can you list the main groups of government revenue, including where oil fits in?
Taxes (like personal income tax, company tax, VAT), oil revenue like royalties and petroleum profit tax, fees and licences, fines, and grants or loans.
Good list. Which of those would you classify as 'borrowing' rather than revenue, and why does that distinction matter?

examples.correct_understanding: Government revenue sources include taxes (personal income tax, company income tax, VAT, customs and excise duties), oil revenue (royalties, petroleum profit tax), fees, licences, fines, rents and grants; loans are borrowings, not revenue.

examples.subject: accounting
examples.source: WAEC-style practice item, Financial Accounting, public sector accounting, objectives
examples.student_opening: Why doesn't the government's financial statement show 'net profit'? Is government not a business?
examples.misconception: Student expects government accounts to measure profit like business accounts.

turns.text: Why doesn't the government's financial statement show 'net profit'? Is government not a business?
Is the goal of a state government borehole project to make profit from villagers, or to provide water for people's welfare?
To provide water — it's a service.
So what do you think public sector accounting mainly tries to show, if not profit?
How public money was collected and spent, and whether spending followed what was approved — accountability, not profit.
Correct. Who are the 'owners' that government is accountable to, and through which body do they usually check the accounts?

examples.correct_understanding: Public sector accounting focuses on stewardship and accountability — showing how public funds were raised and spent in line with approved budgets — rather than profit, because government aims to provide services for public welfare.

examples.student_opening: Isn't the government budget just a guess of what they will spend? Why is it such a big deal every year?
examples.misconception: Student thinks the budget is only a forecast with no legal force over spending.

turns.text: Isn't the government budget just a guess of what they will spend? Why is it such a big deal every year?

Think of a school PTA. At the start of the year, parents approve a plan: ₦500,000 for new desks, ₦200,000 for the library. Could the PTA chairman later spend ₦700,000 on a party without asking the parents?
No — he has to stick to what parents approved, or come back for approval.
Government works similarly. Once the legislature passes the budget as a law, what is that law called, and what does it do to spending?
The Appropriation Act. It authorises how much each ministry can spend, so spending outside it needs further approval, like a supplementary budget.
Correct. Why is this important for controlling public funds, and how does it connect to the Consolidated Revenue Fund?

examples.correct_understanding: The budget, once passed by the legislature as an Appropriation Act, legally authorises government expenditure from the Consolidated Revenue Fund; spending beyond it requires further legislative approval (e.g. a supplementary appropriation). It is a tool of control and accountability, not just a forecast.
